chloe.a: Chloe , also spelled Chloë, Chlöe, or Chloé, is a feminine name meaning "blooming" or "fertility" in Greek. The name ultimately derives, through Greek, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ǵʰelh₃-, which relates to the colors yellow and green.

christian.e: From Middle English Cristien, from Old French chrestien, from Latin Chrīstiānus, from Ancient Greek Χρῑστιᾱνός, from Χρῑστός (“Christ, anointed [one]”) + suffix -ānus. The older form is Christen.
christian.a: Christian is a unisex given name. It originated as a baptismal name used by persons of the Christian religion. It derives from the Latin Christianus, meaning "follower of Christ." It has been used as a given name since the Middle Ages.

christina.e: Name of an early martyr, shortened from Latin Chrīstiāna (“Christian (woman)”).
christina.a: Christina or Cristina is a feminine given name. It is a simplified form of the Latin Christiana, and a feminine form of Christianus or a Latinized form of the Middle English Christin 'Christian' (Old English christen, from Latin). Short forms include Chris and Tina.

christopher.e: From Christophorus, from Χρῑστόφορος (“carrier of Christ”), from Ancient Greek Χριστός (“Christ”) + φόρος (“carrier, bearer”), from φέρειν (“to carry, to bear”) + -ος (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from the legend of Saint Christopher…

cian.e: From Old Irish Cían, from cían (“long, distant, lasting”).
cian.a: Cian is a Gaelic given name meaning "ancient". Cian was the eighth most popular Irish boy's name in Ireland in 2003, and the fourteenth most popular in 2015. Anglicisations of Cian include Kian or Kyan.

ciara.a: Ciara is a popular Irish language female name and was tenth on the list of most popular names given to baby girls in Ireland in 2006.

ciaran.e: From Old Irish Cíarán, originally a byname from ciar + -án. Popularized by Irish saints dating back from the 5th century.
ciaran.a: Ciarán or Ciaran (Scottish Gaelic spelling) is a traditionally male given name of Irish and Scottish origin. It means "little dark one" or "little dark-haired one", produced by appending a diminutive suffix to ciar ("black", "dark"). It is the masculine version of the name Ciara.

ciarrai.a: Kerry or Kerri is a unisex English language given name of Gaelic origin. In its original form Ciarraighe (Ciarraí), it denoted the kingdom of Ciar (ciar raighe), Ciar being the son of Fergus mac Róich, who gave his name to County Kerry.

cillian.e: Irish saint's name, possibly derived from ceallach (“strife”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, strike”)) or ceall (“monastery, church”).
cillian.a: Killian or Kilian, as a given name, is an Anglicized version of the Irish name Cillian. The name Cillian was borne by several early Irish saints including missionaries to Artois (France) and Franconia (Germany) and the author of the life of St Brigid.

claire.e: French Claire, also a spelling variant of the English Clare.
claire.a: Claire or Clair is a given name of French origin. The word means clear in French in its feminine form.

clara.e: Latin clāra, feminine of clārus (“bright, shining, clear”), a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara (Clare) of Assisi.
clara.a: Clara or Klara is a given name. It is the feminine form of the Late Latin name Clarus which meant "clear, bright, famous".

clark.e: From Old English clerc (“clergyman; learned man”), whence also clerk.
clark.a: Clark or Clarke is a given name, a transferred use of the English occupational surname derived from the Latin word clericus, meaning clerk. The name has been in use as a given name in the Anglosphere since the 1600s.

claudia.e: In use from the 16th century. Borrowed from Latin Claudia.
claudia.a: Claudia is a female given name equivalent to Claudius or Claudio. In Portuguese, it is accented Cláudia. A variant and cognate form is Klaudia.

clay.e: From a occupational name for a clay worker, or a habitational name, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”).
clay.a: Clay is both an English surname, and a masculine given name. It may be short for Clayton. Clay (surname)

clayton.e: From Middle English Claytone, Cleyton, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”) + Old English tūn (“enclosure, settlement; town”). Analyzable as clay + ton.
clayton.a: Clayton is both an English surname and a masculine given name. Notable people with the name include:

clementine.e: From Latin clēmentīnus, from Clēmens (“Clement”) (genitive Clēmentis) + -īnus (“of or pertaining to”), from clēmens (“merciful”).
clementine.a: Clémentine or Clementine is a French feminine form of Clement. The name has been in use in English-speaking countries since the 19th century.

cleo.e: Shortened from Cleopatra or a variant of Clio. The rare male name derives from names of Ancient Greek origin such as Cleon and Cleopas.
cleo.a: Cleo is a given name, derived from the name Clio in Greek mythology. As a spelling variant of Clio, the name is etymologically derived from the Greek root κλέω/κλείω, Latinised as kleos (meaning "to recount", "to make famous", "to celebrate", "glory", "to praise" or "to acclaim").

clodagh.a: Clodagh is a female given name of Irish origin. Lady Clodagh Anson, daughter of John Beresford, 5th Marquess of Waterford, was named after the River Clodiagh, which flows through the Marquess's estate at Curraghmore at County Waterford.

clover.a: Clover is a modern given name derived from the common name for the plant, which was ultimately derived from the Old English word clāfre. The name has associations with Ireland and with good fortune due to traditional tales about the Irish shamrock or four-leaf clover.

coby.a: Coby or Koby is a male and female name, a surname, or a nickname originating from the name "Jacob" or "Jakob".

coco.e: From the Italian Coco, a surname derived from cocu (“cook”).
coco.a: Coco is a given name and nickname used by women and men. It may refer to:

coen.a: Coen is a personal name of several origins. It exists as a masculine given name, and as a surname.

cohen.a: Cohen is a masculine given name of Hebrew origin. It derives from the surname of the same spelling, meaning "priest." Cohen is a title associated with hereditary priests, most of whom descended from Aaron, the brother of Moses.

colby.e: From either the personal name Koli or kol (“charcoal”) + býr (“settlement”).
colby.a: Colby is a gender-neutral given name, meaning "Koli's town", "Cola's town", or "coal town".

cole.e: The surname is variously from: # A nickname from Old English col (“coal, coal-black”), # A patronymic from Nicholas (see also Coles, Colson, Colle). # A variation of Cowell (which itself has several origins).
cole.a: Cole is a given name of English origin, originally used as an English surname. It is of Middle English origin, and its meaning is "swarthy, coal-black, charcoal". It is also an Americanized spelling of the German name Kohl, the Dutch name Kool, and the Scottish and Irish name McCool.

coleman.a: Coleman is a masculine given name which may refer to: Coleman Barks , American poet and academic Coleman Bennett (born 2002), American football player Coleman Borthwick (born 2008), American baseball pitcher Coleman Crow (born 2000), American Major League Baseball pitcher Coleman Dowell , American…

colin.a: Colin is an English-language masculine given name. It has two distinct origins: A diminutive form of "Colle", itself an Old French short form of the name Nicolas. This name, but not the anglicized Gaelic name, is also found in the spelling Collin.

colleen.e: From the word colleen, from Irish cailín (“girl”), not used as a name in Ireland. Colleen can also be interpreted as a variant of Coleen, which was a product of marketing by the Hollywood film industry (to promote a new starlet in the…
colleen.a: Colleen is an English-language name of Irish origin. It derives from the Irish word cailín "girl/woman", the diminutive of caile "woman, countrywoman".

colm.e: From Middle Irish Colm, from Columba. Cognate with Scottish Gaelic Calum.
colm.a: Colm is a masculine (and, on rare occasions, a feminine) given name of Irish and Latin origin. It is not an Irish version of Colin, but like Callum and Malcolm derives from a Gaelic variation on columba, the Latin word for "dove".

colman.e: From the saints' name Colmán, diminutive of Colm, from Latin columba (“dove”).
colman.a: Colman or Colmán is a masculine given name which may refer to:

colton.a: Colton is a male given name, and may refer to: Colton Avery (born 1991), American singer and songwriter Colton Beck (born 1990), Canadian ice hockey player Colton Brennan , American football player Colton Brown (born 1991), American judoka Colton Collins (born 2004), American stock car racer Colton…

con.a: Con is a short form of the following given names Cornelius Conrad Constantine Connor or Conor Con is also a given name on its own that may refer to Con Conrad , American songwriter and producer Con Colleano , Australian tightrope walker Con Cremin , Irish diplomat Con Lehane , Irish nationalist Con…

conal.a: Conal is an Irish male given name (and rarely a surname).

conall.e: From Old Irish Conall, from Proto-Celtic *Kunowalos, from *kū (“dog, hound”) + *walos (“prince, chief”).

conan.e: From Irish Conán, from Middle Irish Conán, a derivative of Proto-Celtic *kū (“dog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ.

conchur.a: Conchobar is an old and famous Irish male name meaning "lover of canines". It is the source of the Irish names Conor, Connor, Connors, Conner, O'Connor, etc.

conleth.e: Anglicised from Irish Conlao, Conlaodh, from Old Irish Conláed. Saint Conláed was an Irish hermit and the first Bishop of Kildare.

conn.a: Conn is a masculine English and Irish-language given name, as well as an English-language surname. The origin of the given name is uncertain. It may be related to the Old Irish cond ("intellect", "mind", "king"), or perhaps to the Old Irish cenn ("head", "chief", "queen").

connie.a: Connie () is a given name. It is often a pet form (hypocorism) of Concetta, Constance, Cornelia, Cornelius, Conor, Conrad, Constanza, Concepcion/Conception, Consuela, Consuelo, or Conner.

connor.e: The first name is from Irish Conchúr, Conchobhar, from Old Irish Conchobar (“lover of hounds”). The surname is from Irish Ó Conchúir (“descendant of Conchúr”).
connor.a: Connor is an Irish male given name, anglicised from the compound Irish word Conchobhar, meaning "lover of hounds", or "lover of wolves".

conor.e: From Irish Conchúr, from Old Irish Conchobar (“lover of hounds”).
conor.a: Conor is a male given name of Irish origin. The meaning of the name is "Lover of Wolves" or "Lover of Hounds". Conchobhar/Conchubhar or from the name Conaire, found in Irish legend as the name of the high king Conaire Mór and other heroes.

constance.a: Constance is a primarily feminine given name in use since the Middle Ages that is derived either from Constantia, a Late Latin name, or from the term meaning steadfast. In medieval England, diminutives of the name included Cust or Cussot. Puritans used Con, Constant, and Constancy.

conway.a: Conway is a Welsh, Irish, and Scottish given name, the origin of which is unclear. It may originally have been an Anglicization of Welsh Conwy (derived from Old Welsh cyn "chief" and gwy "water"); of Irish Conbhuidhe or O Connmhachain; or of Scottish Gaelic Mac Conmheadha or Mac Connmhaigh.

cooper.a: Cooper is a masculine given name of English origin. Its meaning is "barrel maker".

cora.e: Apparently brought up in English literature by James Fenimore Cooper in The Last of the Mohicans (1826), but compare a female heroine of this name in Jean-François Marmontel's Les Incas (1777) and the epithet Κόρη for Περσεφόνη.
cora.a: Cora is a given name with multiple origins. It was used by James Fenimore Cooper for a character in his 1826 novel The Last of the Mohicans. It is today most commonly viewed as a variant name derived from the Ancient Greek Κόρη (Kórē), an epithet of the Greek goddess Persephone.

cordelia.e: Shakespeare's spelling of a historical British name appearing as Cordeilla, etc., possibly derived from the saint's name Cordula.
cordelia.a: Cordelia is a feminine given name. It was borne by the tragic heroine of Shakespeare's King Lear (1606), a character based on the legendary queen Cordelia. The name is of uncertain origin.

corey.a: Corey is a masculine given name and a surname. It is a masculine version of name Cora, which has Greek origins and is the maiden name of the goddess Persephone. The name also can have origins from the Gaelic word coire, which means "in a cauldron" or "in a hollow".

cormac.e: From Old Irish Cormac, older Corbmac (see the Old Irish entry).
cormac.a: Cormac is a masculine given name in the Irish and English languages. The name is ancient in the Irish language and is also seen in the rendered Old Norse as Kormákr. Mac is Irish for "son", and can be used as either a prefix or a suffix.

cosmo.e: Borrowed by Scotland from Italy in the 18th century. An variant of Cosimo, from the name Cosmas of a saint (martyred with his brother Damian in the fourth century), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (“order, ordered universe”).
cosmo.a: Cosmo () is a British and Italian surname and unisex given name.

cristian.a: Cristian is the Romanian, Spanish and Italian form of the male given name Christian. In Romanian, it is also a surname. Cristian may refer to:

croia.a: Croía (also Croíadh; both ), are feminine given names derived from the Irish word croí meaning "heart". Croía by 2023 had risen to 23rd most popular girl's name in the Republic of Ireland, and 59th in Northern Ireland.

croiadh.a: Croía (also Croíadh; both ), are feminine given names derived from the Irish word croí meaning "heart". Croía by 2023 had risen to 23rd most popular girl's name in the Republic of Ireland, and 59th in Northern Ireland.

cruz.e: From cruz (“cross”), in the religious sense, and as a topographic surname.
cruz.a: Cruz is primarily a surname, but is also used as a first name mainly in the US and the UK. It is of Iberian origin, first found in Castile, Spain, and later spread throughout the territories of the former Spanish and Portuguese Empires.

curtis.e: From Old French corteis and curteis (Modern French courtois (“polite, courteous”).
curtis.a: Curtis or Curtiss is a common English given name and surname of Anglo-Norman origin, deriving from the Old French curteis (Modern French courtois) which was in turn derived from Latin cohors. Nicknames include Curt, Curty and Curtie. The name means "polite, courteous, or well-bred".

cyrus.e: Latin Cȳrus, from Ancient Greek Κῦρος. As a saints' name it has been identified by folk etymology with Ancient Greek κύριος (“lord”).
cyrus.a: Cyrus is a Persian-language masculine given name. It is historically best known as the name of several Persian kings, most notably Cyrus the Great, who founded the Achaemenid Empire in 550 BC.

dahlia.e: From the flower dahlia in the 19th century.
dahlia.a: Dahlia is a feminine given name derived from the name for the flower, which was named in honor of the Swedish botanist Anders Dahl. His surname is of Germanic origin and refers to a person who lived in a valley.

daire.a: Dáire was a masculine Old Irish name which fell out of use at an early period, remaining restricted essentially to legendary and ancestral figures. It, as well as its unnacented form Daire, has come back into fashion since the 20th century as a unisex alternative spelling of Darragh.

daisy.e: From the flower daisy, one of the flower names dating from the 19th century. Also a nickname for Margaret, since Marguerite and Margarita are identical with the French and Spanish word for "daisy".
daisy.a: Daisy is a feminine given name. The flower name comes from the Old English word dægeseage, meaning "day's eye". The name Daisy is therefore ultimately derived from this source.

daithi.a: Dáithí or Daithí , sometimes also anglicised without diacritics as Daithi, is an Irish male given name which means swiftness or nimbleness. An Icelandic equivalent is Daði.

dakota.a: Dakota is a unisex given name derived from the name of the Native American Dakota people. The name is translated to mean "friend", "friendly" or "allies" in the Yankton-Yanktonai and Santee dialects of the Dakota language.

dalia.a: Dalia is a feminine name. It is used in Arabic , Hebrew , Lithuanian and Persian . The name means "branch," "flower," "gentle," "branch," or "bough of a tree".

dalton.a: Dalton is a masculine given name.

damian.e: From the name Δαμιανός which was derived from δαμάω (“to tame”) (see δαμάζω). Name known in Ancient Greece, later borne by Christian saints.
damian.a: Damian is a given name that comes from Damianus, which is the latinisation of the Greek name Δαμιανός (Damianos), derived from the Greek word δαμάζω (damazō), "(I) conquer, master, overcome, tame", in the form of δαμάω/-ῶ (damaō), a form assumed as the first person of δαμᾷ (damāi).

damien.a: Damien is a given name and less frequently a surname. The name is a variation of Damian which comes from the Greek Damianos.

damir.a: Damir is a male given name.

damon.e: From Ancient Greek Δάμων, a name famous for the story of Damon and Pythias; derivative of δαμάζω (“to tame, subdue”).
damon.a: Damon is a masculine given name. It is the English form of the Greek masculine name Δάμων Damōn, derived from δαμάζειν damazein, meaning "to overpower, tame, subdue, conquer".

dan.a: Dan is a name in various cultures. As a given name it is often short for Daniel. It is also a surname with multiple origins.

dana.e: Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Dawnay, or else an altered form of Dan or Daniel.
dana.a: Dana is a unisex given name. It was among the 100 most popular names given to girls born in the United States between 1960 and 1990. It has since fallen in popularity and was ranked the 446th most popular name given to girls born in the United States in 2007.

daniel.e: From Middle English Daniel, Daniell, from Ancient Greek Δᾱνῑήλ, from Hebrew דָּנִיֵּאל, name borne from the prophet whose story is told in the Book of Daniel.
daniel.a: Daniel is a masculine given name and a surname of Hebrew origin. It means "God is my judge" and derives from two early biblical figures, primary among them Daniel from the Book of Daniel.

daniela.a: Daniela is a feminine given name. Daniela, Daniella or Danniella may refer to:

daniella.a: Daniela is a feminine given name. Daniela, Daniella or Danniella may refer to:

danielle.e: French Danielle, the feminine form of Daniel.
danielle.a: Danielle is a modern French female variant of the male name Daniel. Daniëlle is a Dutch version of the name.

daniyal.a: Daniyal is a given name and surname which may also refer to:

danny.a: Danny is a masculine given name. Notable people with the name include:

dante.a: Dante is an Italian given name and surname. Etymologically, it is short for an old given name, Durante, and was first made popular by the Italian poet Dante Alighieri, whose real name was Durante. Notable people with the name include:

daphne.a: Daphne (or Dafne) is a feminine given name of Greek origin meaning laurel.

dara.e: An Irish saint's name, from Irish Dáire.

darby.e: From the English place name Derby, from Old Norse djúr (“deer”) + býr (“settlement”).
darby.a: Darby is an English locational surname and has since become a given name. Its prefix derives from the Old Norse djúr ("deer"), and the suffix -býr ("farm"/"settlement"). The oldest recorded use as a surname dates to the period of 1160–1182 in Lincolnshire.

darcie.a: Darcie is a feminine given name. Notable people with the name include: Darcie Dohnal (born 1972), American short track speed skater Darcie Lappan (born 2001), Canadian ice hockey player Darcie Vincent (born 1970), women's basketball coach

darcy.e: Originally from Bois-d'Arcy, Yvelines in Northern France. Related to archaic French ardre (“to burn, consume”).

daria.e: Feminine form of Darius, of origin. Name of an early Christian saint.
daria.a: Daria or Darya is a predominantly a feminine version of the Greek name Darius.

darina.a: Darina or Daryna (Ukrainian) is a South Slavic feminine given name. It is common in Bulgarian, Czech, Slovak, Slovenian, Ukrainian,Tatarian cultures and comes from the root Slavic element "dar" which means gift.

darius.e: Borrowed from Latin Dārīus, from Ancient Greek Δᾱρεῖος, shortened form; see there for more.
darius.a: Darius is an English-rendered masculine given name of Persian origin, derived from the original name Dariush .

darla.a: Darla is a female given name of English origin which is a variant of Darlene. Darla means “Darling” Darla may refer to:

darragh.e: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Dubhdarach (“descendant of Dubhdarach”), a personal name composed of the elements dubh (“black”) and darach, genitive of dair (“oak”).
darragh.a: Darragh, also spelled Daragh and Dara, is a name of Irish origin. The name is derived from the Old Irish word daire , which means "oak". Darragh is frequently used in Ireland as a masculine forename, though sometimes occurs as a surname or feminine forename.

darren.a: Darren is a masculine given name of uncertain etymological origins. Some theories state that it originated from an Anglicisation of the Irish first name Darragh or Dáire, meaning "oak tree".

david.e: From Middle English David, Davyd, Davyde, from Old English Dauid, David, from Dāvīd, from Δαυῑ̈́δ, from Biblical Hebrew דָּוִד.
david.a: David is a common masculine given name of Hebrew origin.

dawson.e: From Daw, a pet form of David + son.
dawson.a: Dawson is a masculine given name. Notable people with the name include:

dawud.a: Daud is a male Arabic given name and surname corresponding to David. The Persian form is Davud or Davoud. Other variant spellings in the Latin alphabet include Da'ud, Daut, Daoud, Dawud, Dawood, Davood, Daood and Davut.

deacon.a: Deacon is a male given name of Greek and English origin which means "messenger" or "servant".

deaglan.a: Declan is an Irish given name, an anglicised form of the Irish saint name Declán, also Deaglán or Déaglán. St Declán founded a monastery in Ireland in the 5th century, and the St Declán's stone has been credited as the site of many miracles.

dean.e: The surname or given name is of multiple origins, depending on context:
dean.a: Dean is an English masculine given name and middle name with several origins: Derived from the Greek word "δεκανός" ("dekanos"), which means "monk or dignitary in charge of ten others"

deborah.a: Deborah is a feminine given name derived from דבורה D'vorah, a Hebrew word meaning "bee". Deborah was a prophetess in the Old Testament Book of Judges. In the United States, the name was most popular from 1950 to 1970, when it was among the 20 most popular names for girls.

declan.e: From Old Irish Declán, whence the modern equivalent Deaglán.
declan.a: Declan is an Irish given name, an anglicised form of the Irish saint name Declán, also Deaglán or Déaglán. St Declán founded a monastery in Ireland in the 5th century, and the St Declán's stone has been credited as the site of many miracles.

deirdre.a: Deirdre is a feminine given name of Celtic origin and of unknown meaning. Deirdre is the name of a tragic heroine of Irish mythology. More attention was drawn to the name during the early 20th century in Ireland and throughout the Anglosphere after W.

delia.e: From Ancient Greek Δηλίᾱ, epithet of the goddess Artemis, referring to her birth on the island of Delos.
delia.a: Delia is a feminine given name either taken from an epithet of the Greek moon goddess Artemis, or else representing a short form of Adelia, Bedelia, Cordelia or Odelia. Della is a diminutive form.

delilah.e: Borrowed from Hebrew דְּלִילָה (“[she who] weakened”).
delilah.a: Delilah is a feminine given name of uncertain meaning. The best known Delilah is the Biblical character. The name has been in use in the United States and United Kingdom since the mid-1600s.

demi.a: Demi is a feminine given name with Greek and Latin roots, and it is a surname with Albanian origins. Demi was originally a nickname of Demetria, the feminine form of the masculine name Demetrius, which is itself the Latin and English spelling of the Greek name Demetrios. People named Demi include:

denis.a: Denis is a masculine given name. Notable people with the name include:

deniz.e: Two possible origins: * Deniz, from a variant of the personal name Denís. * Turkish Deniz, an ornamental surname from deniz (“sea”).
deniz.a: Deniz is a unisex Turkish given name meaning "sea". It is used for both women and men. Deniz is the 63rd most popular name among males and the 69th most popular name among females.

dennis.e: From Middle English Denis, from saint's name Denis, brought to England by Normans; from Latin Dionysius, a masculine name literally meaning “follower of (the wine god) Dionysus”.

denny.a: Denny or Dennie is a given name or nickname, primarily masculine and often a short form (hypocorism) of Dennis, Denise, Denver, Denzel, Zdenko, or Zdenka which may refer to:

denver.a: Denver is both an English surname and given name. Notable people with the name include:

denzel.a: Denzel, when used as a male name, ultimately derives from the Cornish language and means "from the high stronghold" or "fertile ground." The manor dates to at least the early 1500s and was described in volume 3 of Magna Britannia (1814) as being the home of an "ancient family of that name".

dermot.a: Diarmaid is a masculine given name in the Irish language, which has historically been anglicized as Jeremiah or Jeremy, names with which it is etymologically unrelated. The name Dimity might have been used as a feminine English equivalent of the name in Ireland.

desmond.a: Desmond is a given name and a surname, derived from the Irish place-name Desmond, an anglicization of the Irish Deas-Mhumhna ("South Munster"). The Irish peerages of Ormonde, Desmond, and Thomond represented the old sub-kingdoms of East, South, and North Munster, respectively.

destiny.e: From the noun destiny since the 1970s.
destiny.a: Destiny is a primarily feminine given name meaning "destiny", "fate", which is ultimately derived from the Late Latin word destinata. Commonly used spelling variants include Destinee, Destiney, and Destinie.

devin.a: Devin is a unisex English-language given name, of many origins. One origin for Devin is from the surname Devin, which is an anglicization of the Irish patronymic Ó Damháin. The Irish patronymic is in reference to the given name 'damán allaid' meaning "fawn", or "poet".

devon.e: From Old English Defenas, which meant both "Devonians" and "Devon," exemplifying the common Anglo-Saxon practice of naming a place after the people who inhabit it.
devon.a: The given name Devon is of uncertain origin. It may be derived from either the English county Devon, or from the surname Devon. A feminine variant of the name is Devonne.

dexter.e: Variant of Dyster. Also partially from Latin dexter (“right (handed)”).
dexter.a: Dexter is an English masculine given name. It is a transferred use of a surname derived from the Old English word deagestre, meaning "dyer of cloth." Dexter is also a Latin term meaning skillful.

diana.e: Borrowed from Diāna, short form of Latin Dīāna, derived by syncope from Dīvāna, equivalent to dīvus + -āna; roughly akin to *deiwā (“goddess”) + Proto-Indo-European *-néh₂.
diana.a: Diana is a feminine given name of Latin and Greek origins, referring to the Roman goddess Diana, goddess of the hunt and the moon.

diarmaid.e: From Old Irish Diarmait; anterior etymology unknown. Possibly from Old Irish dí- (“un-, dis-”) + airmit (“injunction”) (compare áirigh (“to reckon, count”)) or format (“envy”).
diarmaid.a: Diarmaid is a masculine given name in the Irish language, which has historically been anglicized as Jeremiah or Jeremy, names with which it is etymologically unrelated. The name Dimity might have been used as a feminine English equivalent of the name in Ireland.

diarmuid.a: Diarmaid is a masculine given name in the Irish language, which has historically been anglicized as Jeremiah or Jeremy, names with which it is etymologically unrelated. The name Dimity might have been used as a feminine English equivalent of the name in Ireland.

diego.e: Spanish Diego, from an Iberian Didacus, of uncertain origin.
diego.w: List of people with given name Diego
diego.a: Notable people with the given name Diego include:

dillon.e: From the surname, from Breton Leon and Léon, named after Sir Henry de Leon of the Viscounty of Léon. Related to the surname Lyon.
dillon.a: Dillon is a masculine given name.

dion.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δίων. Also a medieval English and French diminutive of Dionysius (Dennis).

diya.a: Diya is a feminine given name and a surname. It is derived from the Sanskrit word ‘diyam’ which means ‘light’ or ‘lamp’. The name Diya symbolizes enlightenment, knowledge, and wisdom.

doireann.a: Doireann is an Irish language feminine given name.

dolly.a: Dolly is a given name and nickname, often a diminutive of the English personal names Dorothy and Dolores.

domhnall.a: Donald is a Scottish masculine given name. It is derived from the Gaelic name Dòmhnall. This comes from the Proto-Celtic *Dumno-ualos ("world-ruler" or "world-wielder").

dominic.a: Dominic, Dominik or Dominick is a male given name common among Roman Catholics and other Latin-Romans. Originally from the late Roman-Italic name "Dominicus", its translation means "Lordly", "Belonging to God" or "of the Master".

dominik.a: Dominic, Dominik or Dominick is a male given name common among Roman Catholics and other Latin-Romans. Originally from the late Roman-Italic name "Dominicus", its translation means "Lordly", "Belonging to God" or "of the Master".

donnacha.a: Donnacha is an Irish given name; a variant of Donnchadh.

donncha.e: From Old Irish Donnchad, from donn (“brown”) and cath (“battle”). Compare Scottish Gaelic Donnchadh.
donncha.a: Donnchadh is a masculine given name common to the Irish and Scottish Gaelic languages. It is composed of the elements donn, meaning "brown" or "dark" from Donn a Gaelic God; and chadh, meaning "chief" or "noble". The name is also written as Donnchad, Donncha, Donnacha, Donnchadha and Dúnchad.

donnchadh.e: From Old Irish Donnchad, from donn (“brown”) plus either cath (“battle”) or cáid (“noble”).
donnchadh.a: Donnchadh is a masculine given name common to the Irish and Scottish Gaelic languages. It is composed of the elements donn, meaning "brown" or "dark" from Donn a Gaelic God; and chadh, meaning "chief" or "noble". The name is also written as Donnchad, Donncha, Donnacha, Donnchadha and Dúnchad.

donnie.a: Donald is a Scottish masculine given name. It is derived from the Gaelic name Dòmhnall. This comes from the Proto-Celtic *Dumno-ualos ("world-ruler" or "world-wielder").

donovan.e: From Irish Ó Donndubháin (“descendant of (a person named) brown & black”), from donn (“brown”) and dubh (“black”).
donovan.a: Donovan is a masculine given name of Irish origin deriving from Ó Donndubháin (brown haired chieftain).Notable people with the name include:

dorian.e: Constructed like the French Doriens. From the root of Dōres + -ian. Compare Ancient Greek Δωριεύς (“of Doris”).
dorian.a: Dorian () is a given name of Greek origin. In Greek, the meaning of the name Dorian is of Doris, a district of Ancient Greece, or of Dorus, a legendary Greek hero. Dorus was a son of Hellen, the eponymous progenitor of the Hellenes.

dorothea.a: Dorothea, also spelt Dorothee (German), Dorothée (French), and Dorotea, is a female given name from Greek Δωροθέα (Dōrothéa) meaning "god's gift". In English it is more commonly spelt Dorothy. People with this name include:

dorothy.a: Dorothy is a feminine given name. It is the English vernacular form of the Greek Δωροθέα (Dōrothéa) meaning 'God's gift', from δῶρον (dōron) 'gift' + θεός (theós) 'god'. It has been in use since the 15th century.

dottie.a: Dottie or Dotty is a feminine given name or nickname (most often a short form of Dorothy) which may refer to:

dougie.a: Douglas is a masculine given name which originated from the surname Douglas. Although today the name is almost exclusively given to boys, it was used as a woman's name in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in the north of England.

douglas.e: From a place name, Scottish Gaelic dubh (“black”) + glais (“stream”).
douglas.a: Douglas is a masculine given name which originated from the surname Douglas. Although today the name is almost exclusively given to boys, it was used as a woman's name in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in the north of England.

drew.a: Drew () is both a surname and a given name. A son of Charlemagne had that name, and it became popular in France as Dreus and Drues. Another source was the county of Dreux, also in France, ruled by the Counts of Dreux from the 12th century onward.

dulcie.e: From Latin dulcis (“sweet”) in the 19th century, probably inspired by earlier names like Dowsabel and Spanish Dulcinea.
dulcie.a: Dulcie is an English feminine given name derived from the Latin dulcis, meaning sweet. It has been in use in the Anglosphere since the 1800s.

dylan.e: From mythology; possibly from for "son of the sea" or "born from the ocean." Unrelated to the name Dillon, although the homophony may result in the two being considered variant spellings of the same name.
dylan.a: Dylan is a given name and surname of Welsh origin. It means "son of the sea", "born from the ocean", or "great tide". It is derived from the Welsh words "dy," meaning "great," and "llanw," meaning "tide" or "sea".

eachann.e: From a derivative of Old Irish Eochaid, from Proto-Celtic *Ekʷo-dixs.
eachann.a: Eachann is a masculine given name in Scottish Gaelic. A similar and possibly related early form of the name was Eachdonn. The name is composed of two elements; the first element is each, meaning "horse".

eadaoin.a: Éadaoin is an Irish feminine given name. It is sometimes anglicised as Aideen. Étaín is the name of a heroine from Irish mythology, and is recorded as being borne by several women between the 12th and 15th century in the Irish annals. It is still in use in 21st century Ireland.

eadie.a: Eadie is a unisex given name. Notable people with the name include: Eadie Adams , American film actress Eadie Fraser , Scottish football player Eadie Wetzel , American swimmer

eala.a: Éala is an Irish feminine given name. It might be influenced by eala, the Irish word for swan. While eala is pronounced with a short a sound, the addition of the síneadh fada alters the pronunciation of the name Éala to Ayla, pronounced with a long a sound.

eamon.a: Eamonn or Eamon , is a masculine Irish given name. It is an Irish form of the English Edmund, or Edward, which are derived from Old English names containing the elements ēad ("prosperity, riches"), mund ("protector") and ward (guard).

eamonn.a: Eamonn or Eamon , is a masculine Irish given name. It is an Irish form of the English Edmund, or Edward, which are derived from Old English names containing the elements ēad ("prosperity, riches"), mund ("protector") and ward (guard).

ebony.e: From ebony. First used by African Americans in the 1970s.
ebony.a: Ebony is an English feminine given name often given in reference to the color black or to the type of wood. It has been particularly well used by Black people in the United States.

eddie.a: Eddie or Eddy is a diminutive for given names such as Edward, Edmund, Edgar, Edison, Edsel, Edwin, Eduardo, Edmundo or Ed. It is also occasionally used as a given name on its own. Notable people known as Eddie or Eddy include:

eden.a: Eden , as a given name is most often given in reference to the Biblical Garden of Eden, meaning delight; it is given to boys and girls. The first recorded use is from ancient Israel in the book of Genesis.

edgar.e: From Old English Ēadgār, the name of early English kings, from Old English ēad (“rich”) + gār (“spear”). Compare Icelandic Auðgeir.
edgar.a: Edgar is a commonly used masculine English given name, from an Anglo-Saxon name Edgar (composed of ead "rich, prosperous" and gar "spear").

edie.a: Edie is a feminine given name, often a diminutive form (hypocorism) of Edith, as well as a surname. It may refer to:

edith.e: Old English Ēadġȳþ, from Proto-Germanic *audaz (“wealth, riches”) + *gunþiz (“battle”). Name of a 10th century English saint.
edith.a: Edith is a feminine given name derived from the Old English word ēad, meaning wealth or prosperity, in combination with the Old English gȳð, meaning strife, and is in common usage in this form in English, German, many Scandinavian languages and Dutch. Its French form is Édith.

edmund.e: From Old English Ēadmund, from ēad (“prosperity”) + mund (“protection”).
edmund.a: Edmund is a masculine given name in the English language. The name is derived from the Old English elements ēad, meaning "prosperity" or "riches", and mund, meaning "protector". Persons named Edmund include:

eduard.a: Eduard is a masculine given name, which is, among other languages, a German, Dutch, and Russian form of the English name Edward.

edward.e: From Middle English Edward, from Old English Ēadweard, from Proto-West Germanic *Audawardu, from Proto-Germanic *Audawarduz, corresponding to ed (“wealth, riches”) + ward (“ward, guard”).
edward.a: Edward is an English masculine name. It is derived from the Anglo-Saxon name Ēadweard, composed of the elements ēad "wealth, fortune; prosperity" and weard "guardian, protector”.

edwin.e: Old English Ēadwine, from Proto-West Germanic *Audawini, from Proto-Germanic *Audawiniz. Akin to Old Norse Auðun, Icelandic Auðunn, German Otwin, Norwegian Audun, and the Lombard king's name Audoin (French Ouen).
edwin.a: The name Edwin means "wealth-friend". It comes from Old English: ēad (wealth, good fortune) and Old English: wine (friend). Thus the Old English form is Ēadwine, a name widely attested in early medieval England.

effie.e: From Euphemia + -ie, very rarely, from modern Greek Eftychia or Euthemia (diminutive form).
effie.a: Effie is a feminine given name, sometimes a short form (hypocorism) of Efthymia , Eftychia , or Euphemia . Notable people with the name include:

eibhlin.e: From Middle English Evelyn, from Old French Aveline, assimilated to the suffix -ín.

eileen.e: From Anglicized forms of Irish Eibhlín, Eilín or Aibhilín in and Modern English, all cognates of from Old French Aveline. Sometimes also used for the Irish name Éibhleann, possibly from Old Irish oíph (“radiance, beauty”).
eileen.a: Eileen ( eye-LEEN or EYE-leen) is an Irish feminine given name anglicised from Eibhlín, an Irish form of the Norman French name Aveline, which is derived from the Germanic Avi, possibly meaning desire in combination with the diminutive suffix el and -in.

eilidh.e: In origin, a diminutive of Eileanor.
eilidh.a: Eilidh is a Scottish Gaelic feminine given name. Although it is the equivalent of Ellie, it is usually anglicized as Helen.

eilish.a: Éilis or Éilís , anglicized as Eilish or Eylish ( AY-lish or EYE-lish), is an Irish given name.

eira.e: From an goddess of medicine, Eir, eir (“relief”). The neighborhood in Helsinki was named after a hospital in the area, in turn named after a hospital in Stockholm, named after the aforementioned goddess.

eithne.e: From Middle Irish Eithne, from Old Irish Eithne.

ela.a: Ela (or Elâ) is a feminine given name of Turkish origin meaning "hazel". Ela is also an Aramaic feminine given name. It comes from the Aramaic word Elah meaning "oak".

elaina.a: Elena is a popular female given name of Greek origin. The name means "shining light". Nicknames of the name Elena are Lena, Lennie, Ella, Ellie, Nellie, or Nena (less common).

eleanor.e: The first known bearer was Eleanor of Aquitaine (1122–1204), Aliénor, perhaps from Latin alia (“other”) and her mother's name Aenor, its meaning thereby said to be “the other Aenor”.
eleanor.a: Eleanor () is a feminine given name, originally from an Old French adaptation of the Old Provençal name Aliénor. It was the name of a number of women of royalty and nobility in western Europe during the High Middle Ages.

elena.a: Elena is a popular female given name of Greek origin. The name means "shining light". Nicknames of the name Elena are Lena, Lennie, Ella, Ellie, Nellie, or Nena (less common).

eleni.a: Eleni is a feminine given name of Greek origin. It is a phonetic spelling of the Modern Greek name "Ελένη", whose ancient version, Ἑλένη, is anglicized as Helen. Popular diminutives and nicknames include: Elenitsa, Elenaki, Elena, Lena, Lenio, Lenners, Nitsa.

eli.e: From Hebrew עֵלִי (“ascent”); cognate to the Arabic-derived Ali.

eliana.a: Eliana, Elianna, אֱלִיעָנָה , Eλιάνα , إليانا , is a feminine given name found with that spelling in Hebrew, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish.

elias.e: The New Testament form of Elijah, a Hebrew prophet, from Ancient Greek Ἠλίας.

elif.e: From Arabic أَلِف (“alif, the first letter of the Arabic alphabet”), itself cognate with Ancient Greek ἄλφα.

elijah.e: From Hebrew אליהו. Compare Joel. See also Arabic إلياس.
elijah.a: Elijah is a masculine given name after the prophet Elijah in the Hebrew Bible. Elijah was among the five most popular names for Black newborn boys in the American state of Virginia in 2022 and again in 2023. In 2022, it was the 37th-most popular name given to boys in Canada.

elin.e: Medieval variant of Helene (Helen), comparable to English Ellen.

elina.a: Elina is a feminine given name in various languages. It is often considered a form of Helen in different languages such as Estonian, Finnish, and Swedish. Eliina is an alternate Estonian and Finnish spelling.

elio.a: Elio is an Italian male given name.

elis.e: Short form of Eliisabet or Elisabeth.
elis.a: Elis is a given name, used for both men and women.

elisa.a: Elisa is a feminine and masculine (though not as common) given name. It is of Phoenician origin. According to legend, the first queen of Carthage was Elissa (also known as Dido).

elise.e: From French Élise or German Elise, both variants of Elisabeth.

eliza.a: Eliza is a female given name in English, meaning "pledged to God" or "joyful."

elizabeth.e: From Middle English Elizabeth, from the Ancient Greek Ἐλισάβετ, a transliteration of the Old Testament Biblical Hebrew אלישבע (“my God is an oath”). See El and שבועה.
elizabeth.a: Elizabeth is a feminine given name, a variation of the Hebrew name Elisheva , meaning "My God is an oath" or "My God is abundance", as rendered in the Septuagint.

ella.e: A 19th-century shortening of Eleanor or Ellen, later also used for any name ending in -ella, such as Gabriella or Daniella.
ella.a: Ella is a personal name most often used as a feminine given name, but also as a surname, especially in Australia. In Greek mythology, Ella was the daughter of Athamas and Nephele.

elle.a: Elle is a female given name. Notable people and characters with the name include:

ellen.e: Medieval English variant of Helen, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη; also used as a variant of Eleanor or a feminine counterpart to Elliot.
ellen.a: Ellen is a feminine given name. It was the 609th most popular name in the U.S. and the 17th in Sweden in 2004. People named Ellen include:

elliana.a: Eliana, Elianna, אֱלִיעָנָה , Eλιάνα , إليانا , is a feminine given name found with that spelling in Hebrew, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish.

ellie.a: Ellie or Elly is a given name.

elliot.a: Elliot (also spelled Eliot, Elliotte, Elliott, Eliott and Elyot) is a personal name that can serve as either a surname or a given name. Although the given name has historically been given to males, females have increasingly been given the name as well in the United States.

elliott.e: English surname derived from a Middle English diminutive of Elie, Old French form of Elias or Elijah, meaning "my God is Yahweh". As a Scottish surname it may also represent Gaelic Elloch from a word meaning a dam or bank.
elliott.a: Elliot (also spelled Eliot, Elliotte, Elliott, Eliott and Elyot) is a personal name that can serve as either a surname or a given name. Although the given name has historically been given to males, females have increasingly been given the name as well in the United States.

ellis.a: Ellis is a given name of Welsh and English origin. Notable people with the given name include:

elodie.a: Élodie is a French feminine given name, a variant of Alodia, possibly a Gothic name with elements Ala, perhaps meaning 'other' or 'all', and od, 'wealth, heritage'. The given name was popularized via veneration of Saint Alodia, a 9th-century child martyr.

eloise.e: From French Éloïse, from the and French forms that gave rise to its doublet.
eloise.a: Eloise is a female given name, the English version of the French name Éloïse or Héloïse . It is of uncertain meaning but may be derived from the Old German name Helewidis , which meant "healthy" and "wide". References are made also to the god Helios, referring the name to the sun.

elora.a: Elora is a feminine given name of uncertain origin. It has become better known as the name of a child character in the 1988 fantasy film Willow. It might be a variant of the names Eliora, a Hebrew name meaning “God is my light”, or Elnora, an American combination of the names Ella and Nora.

elouise.e: Alternative form of Eloise, influenced by Louise.

elsa.e: From German Elsa, contraction of Elisabeth, occasionally used in English after its appearance in Wagner's opera Lohengrin (1847). The common noun is after the character of the Frozen series of films.
elsa.a: Elsa is a female name mostly used in the Scandinavian countries.

elsie.e: From a Scottish diminutive of Alison/Alice and Elspeth/Elizabeth.
elsie.a: Elsie is a feminine given name, a diminutive form of Elspeth, a Scottish version of Elizabeth. It has been in use in the Anglosphere as an independent name since the 1800s. The name has increased in usage in English-speaking countries in recent years.

elspeth.a: Elspeth or Elspet is a feminine given name, which is the Scottish form of Elizabeth. It means "chosen by God" or "consecrated by God". The name may refer to:

elvis.e: From the anglicisation of the Irish name of Saint Ailbe, also known as Saint Eilfyw or Eilfw. Ultimate origin is uncertain.
elvis.a: Elvis is a male given name that is said to have first appeared as that of a Saint Elvis, a figure said to be active in medieval Wales. While the name features in early Medieval Welsh literature and is of Celtic origin, it is uncertain if the name was originally Irish (Gaelic) or Welsh (Brythonic).

ema.a: Emma is a feminine given name. It is derived from the Germanic word ermen, meaning "whole" or "universal". It likely originated as a short form of names such as Ermengarde or Ermentrude.

emanuel.e: Variant of Emmanuel, borrowed from and from various other European languages.
emanuel.a: Emanuel is a masculine given name, the Portuguese, Romanian, Spanish, Czech, Dutch, German, Hungarian, Croatian, Scandinavian form of the English name Emmanuel. The name Emanuel is quite popular in Brazil and has become more common than its primary form, Manuel (Manoel in archaic Portuguese).

emelia.a: Emelia is a feminine first name. Notable people with it are:

emer.e: From Old Irish Emer; cognate with Irish Eimhear and Scottish Gaelic Eimhir.

emerson.a: Emerson is an English given name, a transferred use of an English surname coming either from Anglo-Saxon Emars sunu, "Emar's son," or from "Emery's son." (See also Emerson (surname).) It is in use for both boys and girls. Spelling variants such as Emersyn are also in regular use.

emil.e: From German Emil, from Latin Aemilius, a Roman family name possibly from aemulus (“rival”). Cognate with French Émile.
emil.a: The name Emil, Emile, or Émile is a male given name of Indo-European origin. This name has multiple meanings: laborious, rival, or eager, which are derived from the Latin Aemilius of the gens Aemilia.

emilia.a: Emilia is a female Italian given name of Latin origin. The name is popular all over Europe and the Americas. The corresponding male given name is Emilio.

emilie.e: From Latin Aemilia. Cognate with English Emily.
emilie.a: Émilie (French pronunciation: [emili]) is a French female given name. It is the feminine form of the male name Émile.

emilio.a: Emilio is a given name common in the Italian and Spanish languages. The Portuguese-language version of the name is spelled Emílio. Like its counterpart in other languages, Emil, the name is derived from the Latin Aemilius of the gens Aemilia.

emily.e: English form of Latin Aemilia, a gens name from aemulus (“rival, emulator”).
emily.a: Emily is a feminine given name derived from the Roman family name "Aemilius", and is the feminine form of the name Emil.

emir.a: Emir is a male given name. It is derived from the Arabic title Emir or Amir. In Turkish, Emir means command, order, prince, local king.

emma.e: Brought to England by the Normans; short form of compound given names beginning with a Frankish prototheme Ermin- or Irmin- "entire", from Proto-Germanic *ermunaz.
emma.a: Emma is a feminine given name. It is derived from the Germanic word ermen, meaning "whole" or "universal". It likely originated as a short form of names such as Ermengarde or Ermentrude.

emmeline.e: Medieval English form of Old French Ameline, diminutive form of Amélie, cognate to English Amelia.
emmeline.a: Emmeline (also spelled Emeline, Emiline, Emilene, Emmilene, Emmaline, Emmalyn, Emalyn, or Ameline) is a feminine given name. The medieval name, a short form of Germanic names beginning with the element amal meaning "work", was introduced to England by the Normans.

emmett.e: From a diminutive of the female given name Emma.
emmett.a: Emmett is a unisex given name primarily used for males, and is also used as a surname.

emmy.a: Emmy is a feminine (sometimes also masculine) given name. Orthographic variants include Emme, Emmi and Emmie.

emrys.e: From *Ėmrös, from Latin Ambrosius, from Ancient Greek ἀμβρόσιος (“immortal, divine”).

ena.a: Ena is a given name, nickname, and surname. Notable people and characters with the name include:

enid.e: From Middle Welsh eneit (“spirit, life; purity”), from Proto-Celtic *anatyom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”). Cognate with anatia (“souls (?)”) attested on the Larzac tablet
enid.a: Enid is a feminine given name. Its origin is Middle Welsh eneit, meaning 'spirit; life; purity' .

enola.e: Created for the titular character in the 1886 American novel Enola, derived from alone spelled backwards.
enola.a: Enola is an English feminine given name often taken from the English word alone spelled backwards. It is also an English spelling of a Cherokee name meaning black fox.

enzo.e: Borrowed from Italian Enzo (equivalent to English Hank), from German Heinz, a diminutive of Heinrich (English Henry), from Old High German Heimrih, Haimirich (heim (“home”) + rihhi (“ruler”)), from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks, from roots.
enzo.a: Enzo is an Italian given name derivative of the German name Heinz. It can be used also as the short form for Lorenzo, Vincenzo, Innocenzo, or Fiorenzo. It is most common in the Romance-speaking world, particularly in Italy and Latin America.

eoghain.a: Éogan is an early Irish male given name, which also has the hypocoristic and diminutive forms Eoganán, Eóghainin, Eóghain and Eóghainn. The Modern Irish form of the name is Eoghan . In Scottish Gaelic, the name is Eòghann or Eòghan.

eoghan.e: From Middle Irish Eógan, from Proto-Celtic *Iwogenos. Cognate with Scottish Gaelic Eòghann.
eoghan.a: Éogan is an early Irish male given name, which also has the hypocoristic and diminutive forms Eoganán, Eóghainin, Eóghain and Eóghainn. The Modern Irish form of the name is Eoghan . In Scottish Gaelic, the name is Eòghann or Eòghan.

eoin.e: From Old Irish Iohain, from Latin Iōannēs, from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן.
eoin.a: Eóin is a masculine Irish-language given name. The Scottish Gaelic equivalent is Eòin and both are closely related to the Welsh Ioan. It is also cognate with the Irish Seán and English John.

eren.a: Eren is a popular Turkish and Kazakh male name meaning "saint", "wise", "brave", and "well-educated". The name is Muslim and it's a reference to notable people in Islamic history. Eren is also a Celtic name, denoting a few places in Scotland.

eric.e: From Middle English Eric, from Old English Eoric, from Old Norse Eirríkr, Eiríkr, or from Proto-Germanic *Aizarīkijaz. Less likely from einn + ríkr, from Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king”).

erica.e: A feminine form of Eric, ultimately. The name has also been associated with the flower genus.
erica.a: The given name Erika is a female name with multiple meanings of Classical Latin, Old Norse, and Japanese origin. Erika and the variants Erica, Ericka, or Ereka are feminine forms of Eric, derived from the Old Norse name Eiríkr (or Eríkr in Eastern Scandinavia due to monophthongization).

erik.e: A spelling variant of Eric, or directly borrowed from modern Swedish Erik.

erika.e: Spelling variant of Erica, the feminine form of Eric, or borrowed directly from modern Scandinavia, ultimately from Old Norse Eiríkr.
erika.a: The given name Erika is a female name with multiple meanings of Classical Latin, Old Norse, and Japanese origin. Erika and the variants Erica, Ericka, or Ereka are feminine forms of Eric, derived from the Old Norse name Eiríkr (or Eríkr in Eastern Scandinavia due to monophthongization).

ernest.e: Borrowed in the 18th century from Ernst, a medieval royal name in Germany, from Old High German ernust (“vigor, strife”), only remotely related to modern German ernst or English earnest.
ernest.a: Ernest is a given name derived from the Germanic word ernst, meaning "serious", often shortened to Ernie. Notable people and fictional characters with the name include:

ernie.a: Ernie is a masculine given name, frequently a short form (hypocorism) of Ernest, Ernald, Ernesto, or Verner. It may refer to:

esa.e: Medieval vernacular form of Esaias, the old biblical equivalent of Isaiah. It has also been recorded as a diminutive of Esko and Esau.
esa.a: Esa is a masculine given name of Finnish origin and a surname. Notable people with the name include:

esme.a: Esmé (commonly Esme) or Esmée is a given name derived from the past participle of the Old French verb esmer, "to esteem", thus signifying "esteemed", or similarly "beloved". Originally a masculine name, Esmé had become a feminine name by the mid-twentieth century.

esmee.e: Anglicized spelling of the French Esmée or Esmé
esmee.a: Esmé (commonly Esme) or Esmée is a given name derived from the past participle of the Old French verb esmer, "to esteem", thus signifying "esteemed", or similarly "beloved". Originally a masculine name, Esmé had become a feminine name by the mid-twentieth century.

estelle.e: French Estelle, from estela (“star”), from Latin stēlla. Name of a third century martyr.
estelle.a: Estelle is a female name of Occitan origin, and means star. Saint Estelle was a martyr who purportedly lived in Aquitania in the third century AD, although the earliest references to her date from the Middle Ages.

esther.e: From Ancient Greek Ἐσθήρ, from Biblical Hebrew אֶסְתֵּר. Has been connected to (whence 𐭮𐭲𐭫 (“star”), 𐭮𐭲𐭠𐭫𐭪 (“star”), Persian ستاره (“star”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr (if so, a distant); or else to (Hebrew עִשְׁתָּר).

ethan.a: Ethan or Eytan is a male given name of Hebrew origin that means "firm, enduring, strong and long-lived". The name Ethan appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible (1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 2:6, 8; 6:42, 44; 15:17, 19; Psalm 89 superscription).

etta.a: Etta is an English given name that is a diminutive form of Antonietta, Henrietta and other names that end in “-etta”. Etta is also a Danish, Finnish, Norwegian, Old Danish, Old Swedish and Swedish given name. Notable people with this name include the following:

ettie.a: Etty, Ettie or Etti is a feminine given name, often a short version of Esther. It is also a surname. It may refer to the following people:

euan.a: Euan is a Scottish, male given name, most common throughout the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, due to the influence of Scots in both nations.

eva.e: The (Vulgate) Latin Eva, from Ancient Greek Εὔα, from חַוָּה. A Latinate variant of the English Eve.
eva.a: Eva is a female given name derived from the Greek Εὕα (Heúa), and ultimately from the Hebrew חַוָּה , the name of the first woman in the Book of Genesis. The name spread widely in Europe through the Latin Bible and remains common in many languages.

evan.e: Anglicization of Welsh Ifan, ultimately from Latin Jōhannēs, variant of Iōannēs, from Ἰωάννης, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן.
evan.a: Evan is a Welsh and English masculine given name, derived from Iefan, a Welsh form of the name John. Evan can also occasionally be found as a shortened version of Greek names like Evangelos, Evander, or Evandro.

evangeline.e: Invented by the poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow when he began research on his epic poem Evangeline about Acadian lovers deported from French-Canada. From Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (“good news”).
evangeline.a: Evangelina and Evangeline are feminine given names, diminutives of Latin "evangelium" . People with these names include:

eve.e: From Middle English Eve, Eue, from Old English Ēua, Ēfe, from Latin Eva, from Ancient Greek Εὔα, from Biblical Hebrew חַוָּה.
eve.a: Eve is a feminine English given name, derived from the Latin name Eva, in turn originating with the Hebrew חַוָּה . In Greece the name Eve is Evi , a diminutive of the baptismal name Paraskevi.

evelina.a: Evelina is a feminine given name. It is either a Latinised variant of Evelyn or an extension of Eva. Notable people with the name include:

evelyn.e: From forms of the female name Aveline, diminutive of the root *avi-, of uncertain meaning, possibly “desired, wished for“ (compare Latin avēre, "to wish for") or aval “strength”.
evelyn.a: Evelyn is a matronymic English surname derived from the medieval girl's name Aveline (which is of Norman origin and represents a diminutive form of Ava). Since the 17th century, it has also been used as a given name.

everleigh.e: From Old English eofor (“wild boar”) + lēah (“woodland clearing”). Compare the toponym Everlo.

everly.e: Habitational surname, from a variant of Everleigh.
everly.a: Everly is a given name of English origin that is a transferred use of an English place name and surname. It has increased in popularity as a given name for girls in recent years in the United States.

evie.a: Evie is a feminine given name, diminutive of Eve and Evelyn, and often a short form (hypocorism) of another, such as Evangeline, Evangelina, Evita or the French Geneviève. Evie may refer to:

ewan.e: From Scottish Gaelic Eòghan. Not related to Iwan and Evan.

eyad.a: Eyad is an Arabian given name that may refer to one of the following people: Eyad Hammoud (born 2001), Lebanese footballer Eyad Ismoil (born 1971), Jordanian terrorist who took part in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing Eyad al-Sarraj (1944-2013), Palestinian psychiatrist Eyad Elbayoumi (born…

ezekiel.e: From Ἰεζεκιήλ, from Biblical Hebrew יְחֶזְקֵאל (“God strengthens”).
ezekiel.a: Ezekiel is a masculine Hebrew language name, meaning "God's Strength." It can be used as both a given name and a surname.

ezra.a: Ezra is a masculine given name of Hebrew origin, derived from the root ע־ז־ר meaning 'help'. The name originated from the Biblical figure Ezra the Scribe, who is traditionally credited as the author of Ezra–Nehemiah and the Books of Chronicles of the Hebrew Bible.

fabian.e: From Latin Fabiānus (“belonging to Fabius”), derived from Fabius + -ānus.

faith.a: Faith is an English feminine given name derived from the word faith. It became popularized when the Puritans began using it as a virtue name during the 17th century.

fallon.e: Reduced Anglicized form of Irish Ó Fallamhain (“descendant of Fallamhan”), a personal name related to follúnaitheoir (“ruler, governor”).
fallon.a: Fallon is a given name of the following people: Fallon Bowman (born 1983), South African born Canadian musician Fallon Fox (born 1975), American mixed martial arts fighter Fallon Kelly , United States Attorney Fallon King (born 1988), American singer and member of Cherish Fallon Sherrock (born…

farah.a: Farah is an Arabic- and Persian-language feminine given name meaning "joy" in the former and "glory" in the latter.

faris.a: Faris is an Arabic masculine given name and surname. In Arabic, Faris translates to "knight." In the Balkans, Faris is popular among Bosniaks in the former Yugoslav nations. It is similar to other popular names in the region, such as Haris and Daris.

farrah.e: Variant of Farrar, from Middle English ferreor (“iron worker, smith”). The given name was popularized by the American actress Farrah Fawcett (1947-2009). Her name is often interpreted as a variant of Farah.
farrah.a: Farah is an Arabic- and Persian-language feminine given name meaning "joy" in the former and "glory" in the latter.

fatima.a: Fatima , also spelled Fatimah, is a female given name of Arabic origin used throughout the Muslim world. Several relatives of the Islamic prophet Muhammad had the name, including, most famously, his daughter Fatimah bint Muhammad.

fatimah.a: Fatima , also spelled Fatimah, is a female given name of Arabic origin used throughout the Muslim world. Several relatives of the Islamic prophet Muhammad had the name, including, most famously, his daughter Fatimah bint Muhammad.

faye.a: Faye is a given name in various cultures. In the West, the given name is usually feminine. Faye is derived from Middle English "faie", meaning "fairy", or possibly from the Old French word meaning loyalty or belief.

fearghal.a: Fearghal is an Irish male given name. The name is from the Irish words fear 'man' and gal 'valour', thus the name translates to 'man of valour'. The anglicised form is Fergal or Feargal.

fearghus.a: Fergus or Feargus is a common and one of the oldest known Irish or Scottish male given name derived from Old Irish, meaning "the strong (one)" or "the masculine (one)". As a surname, Ferguson or Fergusson is common across Scotland but particularly in Perthshire and Ayrshire.

fearne.a: Fearne is a given name and a surname.

feilim.a: Féilim or Feidhlim, is an Irish language masculine given name. The name is derived from the older form Feidhlimidh . Féilim has been variously anglicised as Felim, Phelim, Feilmy, Philip or Felix.

felicity.e: From the noun felicity, and also the English form of Latin Felicitas, a name borne by early martyrs.
felicity.a: Felicity is a feminine given name of English origin meaning "happiness". It is derived from the Latin word felicitas meaning "luck, good fortune". It is also used as a form of the Latin name Felicitas, taken from the name of the Ancient Roman goddess Fortuna.

felix.a: Felix is a masculine given name that originates from the Latin word felix [ˈfeːliːks] , meaning "happy", "lucky", "fortunate", "successful", or "fruitful". Its original meaning was "fruit-bearing", in reference to fruitful trees, arbor felix. The feminine forms are Felicia or Felicity.

fergus.e: From or Scottish Gaelic Fearghas. The first element may be related to modern fìor (“true”) or fear (“man”) (cf. Fearchar). The second element has been understood to mean 'choice' (cf. Angus).
fergus.a: Fergus or Feargus is a common and one of the oldest known Irish or Scottish male given name derived from Old Irish, meaning "the strong (one)" or "the masculine (one)". As a surname, Ferguson or Fergusson is common across Scotland but particularly in Perthshire and Ayrshire.

fern.e: From fern; in the case of the surname, it was given to someone who lived in a place where there was an abundance of these plants.
fern.a: Fern is an English topographic name from the Old English fearn. It refers to someone who lives among ferns. The name is used as a given name and a surname.

ffion.a: Ffion [ˈfiː.ɔn] is a Welsh feminine given name meaning foxglove.

fiachra.e: From Old Irish Fíachrai, from Proto-Celtic *Weikorīxs.
fiachra.a: Fiachra is an Irish male given name. It may refer to:

fiadh.e: From fiadh, pre-reform spelling of fia, from Old Irish fíad (“wild; game, deer”).
fiadh.a: Fiadh is an Irish/Scottish feminine given name. In Irish, it is an archaic variant of fia meaning "wild" or "wild game", especially "deer", or—via another etymology—"respect".

fidelma.e: A Latinization of Middle Irish Fedelm, altered under the influence of Latin fidēs (“faith”).
fidelma.a: Fidelma is an Irish female given name, a Latinization of Fedelm.

filip.a: Filip is a masculine given name and a surname, cognate to Philip. The male name Filip comes from the Greek "philos" (love) and "hippos" (horse), which means "horse lover". In Croatia, the name Filip was among the most common masculine given names in the 2000s.

finlay.e: Anglicized from Scottish Gaelic Fionnlagh (“fair warrior/hero”).
finlay.a: Finlay is a masculine given name, and also a surname. The given name is represented in Scottish Gaelic as Fionnlagh.

finley.a: Finley is both a surname and given name.

finn.a: Finn is a masculine given name. The name has several origins. In some cases it is derived from the Old Norse personal name and byname Finnr, meaning "Sámi" or "Finn".

finnegan.e: Borrowed from Irish Ó Fionnagáin (“descendant of Fionnagán”). Fionnagán is a given name that descends from Old Irish Finnacán, which is typically anglicised as Finnegan itself.

finnian.e: From, variant of Fionnán; see fionn (“fair”).

fintan.a: Fintan is an Irish given name. In Irish mythology, Fintan mac Bóchra is said to be the sole survivor of the Great Flood on the island of Ireland, subsequently becoming a personification of old age and knowledge.

fionn.e: From Old Irish Finn, an epithet from the adjective find (“white, bright, fair, handsome”).
fionn.a: Fionn is a masculine given name in Irish and Scottish Gaelic. In English, it is pronounced "Fyun". It is derived from a byname meaning "white" or "fair-haired".

fionnbharr.e: From Middle Irish Finnbarr, from Old Irish Findbarr.

fletcher.e: English occupational surname from the noun fletcher (“arrow-maker”). Sometimes confused with Flesher.
fletcher.a: Fletcher is a masculine given name, which may refer to:

fleur.e: French fleur (“flower”), name of a character in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga.
fleur.a: Fleur is a feminine given name originated in France, eventually used in English speaking countries and other languages. It means "flower" in French.

flora.a: Flora is a feminine given name of Latin origin meaning flower, ultimately derived from the Latin word flos, which had the genitive floris. Flora was a fertility goddess of flowers and springtime in Ancient Rome.

florence.e: French Florence, from Latin Flōrentia (as a given name, a feminine form of Flōrentius), from flōrens (“flowering, flourishing”), from flōs (“flower”), connected with English bloom and blossom.
florence.a: Florence is usually a feminine given name. It is derived from the French version of (Saint) Florentia, a Roman martyr under Diocletian. The Latin florens, florentius means "blossoming", verb floreo, meaning "I blossom / I flower / I flourish".

flynn.e: Anglicized from Irish Ó Floinn, "descendant of Flann (red)".
flynn.a: Flynn is an Irish surname or first name, an anglicised form of the Irish Ó Floinn or possibly Mac Floinn, meaning "descendant or son of Flann" (a byname meaning "reddish (complexion)" or "ruddy"). The name is more commonly used as a surname than a first name.

forest.a: Forest is both a French surname and a given name. Notable people with the name include:

forrest.e: English surname, from the noun forest. Also adopted and translated from the word for "forest" in various other languages by settlers.
forrest.a: Forrest is a masculine given name. Notable persons with the name include: Forrest (singer) , born Forrest Thomas, American singer popular in the UK and Netherlands Forrest J.

fox.a: Fox is a unisex, primarily masculine, given name, a transferred use of the English surname meaning “fox.” In some instances, it might have been used as a given name in honor of George Fox , the founder of the Quaker movement.

frances.e: From Old French Franceise, feminine form of Franceis, from Franciscus (“Frankish”).
frances.a: Frances is an English given name or last name of Latin origin. In Latin the meaning of the name Frances is 'from France' or 'the French.' The male version of the name in English is Francis.

francesca.e: Borrowed from Italian Francesca (“Frances”), the feminine form of Francesco (“Francis”), from Franciscus, from Francia + -iscus.
francesca.a: Francesca is an Italian female given name, derived from the Latin male name Franciscus meaning 'the Frenchman' It is widely used in most Romance languages, including Italian, French and Catalan, and place of origin is Italy.

francis.a: Francis is an English, French, German, Dutch and Scandinavian given name of Latin origin. Francis is a name that has many derivatives in most European languages.

franciszek.a: Franciszek is a masculine given name of Polish origin (female form Franciszka). It is a cognate of Francis, Francisco, François, and Franz.

frank.e: From Middle English Frank, partially from Old English Franca (“a Frank”); and partially from Old French Franc, and/or Latin Francus (“a Frank”), from *Franko (“a Frank”); both maybe from Proto-Germanic *frankô (“javelin”).
frank.a: Frank is a masculine given name.

franklin.e: From Middle English frankelein (“freeholder”), see franklin. The place names are mostly.
franklin.a: Franklin is a masculine English given name. It is of English coming from the medieval English Frankeleyn, coming from the Anglo-Norman fraunclein. Its meaning is landowner of free but not noble origin.

fraser.e: Scottish surname thought to be, but not corresponding to any obvious places in France; perhaps a corrupted transcription of a name. More at Fraser.

fred.a: Fred, sometimes spelled Fredd, is a masculine given name. It is often short for Frederick, Manfred, Alfred, or Wilfred.

freddy.a: Freddy (also Freddi and Freddie) is a unisex given name. It is often used by both men and women whose names contain the Germanic element -fred, such as Frederick, Frederica, and Alfred.

frederick.e: From German Friedrich, Friederich and influenced by Latin Friderīcus, Frederīcus, from Old High German Fridurih, from *Friþurīk, from Proto-Germanic *Friþurīks, from *friþuz + *rīks.
frederick.a: Frederick is a male given name meaning "peace king" or "peaceful ruler". It is the English form of the German name Friedrich. Its meaning is derived from the Germanic word elements frid, or peace, and ric, meaning "king", "ruler", or "power".

fredrick.a: Frederick is a male given name meaning "peace king" or "peaceful ruler". It is the English form of the German name Friedrich. Its meaning is derived from the Germanic word elements frid, or peace, and ric, meaning "king", "ruler", or "power".

freya.e: Scottish form of Old Norse Freyja (“mistress, lady”).
freya.a: Freya or Freyja is an Old Norse feminine given name derived from the name of the Old Norse word for noble lady (Freyja). The theonym of the goddess Freyja is thus considered to have been an epithet in origin, replacing a personal name that is now unattested.

freyja.e: From Old Norse Freyja, from freyja (“lady”), from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ.
freyja.a: Freya or Freyja is an Old Norse feminine given name derived from the name of the Old Norse word for noble lady (Freyja). The theonym of the goddess Freyja is thus considered to have been an epithet in origin, replacing a personal name that is now unattested.

frida.a: Frida (with variants Freda, Freida, Frieda, Frinta) is a feminine given name. In central and eastern Europe, Frida is a short form of compound names containing the Germanic element fried meaning "peace".

fynn.a: Fynn is a surname and given name.

gabriel.e: From Latin Gabriel, from Γαβρῑήλ, from Biblical Hebrew גַּבְרִיאֵל, from גֶּבֶר (“man”) or the triliteral root ג־ב־ר (“strength, manliness”), ־י (“me, my, -'s”), and אֵל (“God, god”), from *ʾil-.
gabriel.a: Gabriel is a given name from various borrowings of the Biblical Hebrew name of the archangel Gaḇrīʾēl , meaning "God is my strength".

gabriela.a: Gabriela is a feminine given name that appears in Portuguese, Spanish, Czech, Slovak, Romanian, Latvian, Polish and Bulgarian. It is a form of the Hebrew name Gabriel, meaning "God is my strength". Related names include Gabriella, Gabriele, Gabrielė, Gabrielle, Gabi and Gabe.

gabriella.a: Gabriella is a feminine given name used in various languages. Its English spelling originates as an Italian feminine given name from the Hebrew name Gabriel. Girls who are named Gabriella often take on a shorter version of the name, such as Bella, Ella, Gab, Gabby, Gabbie and Gabbi.

gabrielle.e: French Gabrielle, feminine form of Gabriel (see there for more).
gabrielle.a: Gabrielle is the French feminine form of the given name Gabriel which translates to "God is my strong man".

gaia.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Γαῖᾰ (“Gaea, the Earth personified as a goddess”), from γαῖᾰ (“the Earth”), probably related to γῆ (“earth, land; country”).

garrett.e: A medieval English and Irish form of the given names Gerard and Gerald. Of Old High German origin.
garrett.a: Garrett is a surname and given name of Germanic and of Old French origins. It is one of the many baptismal surnames to have been derived from the popular given names of Gerardus, Gerard and Gerald in 12th-century England.

gavin.e: Medieval variant of Gawain, the name of an Arthurian knight, first recorded as Gauvain. The form Gavin survived in Scotland and spread to other English-speaking countries in the 1960s.
gavin.a: Gavin is a Celtic male given name. It is the Scottish variation of the medieval Welsh name Gawain, meaning 'God send' or 'white hawk/falcon'. Sir Gawain is a knight of King Arthur's Round Table.

gene.a: Gene is a unisex given name. It is often a short form (hypocorism) of Eugene or Genevieve. Notable people with the name include:

genevieve.e: Borrowed from French Geneviève, from Latin Genovefa, Genoveva, possibly either of origin, ultimately from *kunją + *wībą, or of origin, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *genos (“family, clan”).
genevieve.a: Genevieve (French: Geneviève) is a female name of "Celtic or Germanic origin, possibly from the Germanic name Kenowefa [Latinized as Genoveva], meaning kin, 'race' or 'tribe', and wefa, 'woman'". Genevieve can also mean "woman of the family".

george.e: Name of an early saint, from Middle English George, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργῐος, from γεωργός (“farmer, earth worker”), from γῆ (“earth”) (combining form γεω-) + ἔργον (“work”).
george.a: George (English: ) is a male given name derived from the Greek name Georgios . It may have been a theophoric name, with origins in Zeus Georgos, an early title of the Greek god Zeus.

georgia.a: Georgia is a feminine given name originating from the Greek word Γεωργία (Georgía), meaning "agriculture". It shares this origin with the masculine version of the name, George.

georgie.a: Georgie is a unisex given name, often a hypocorism of Georgina, Georgiana, or George. Bearers of the name include:

georgina.e: From George + -ina, feminine form of George.
georgina.a: Georgina is a given name and the feminine form of George, along with Georgia and Georgiana. It comes from the Greek word γεωργός , meaning "farmer".

gerard.e: From Middle English Gerard, from Old French Gerart, from *Gaiʀahard, from *gaiʀ + *hard(ī).
gerard.a: Gerard is a masculine forename of Proto-Germanic origin, variations of which exist in many Germanic and Romance languages. Like many other early Germanic names, it is dithematic, consisting of two meaningful constituents put together.

gia.a: Gia is an English female given name, used as short for the Italian name Gianna (English Jane), Giada (English Jade) or Georgia.

gianna.a: Gianna is a female Italian given name, a diminutive form of Giovanna. In English, it is translated as "Jane", "Jean", "Joan", "Joanne" or "Joanna".

gideon.a: Gideon is a gender neutral given name and surname of Hebrew origin which translates to 'feller' or 'hewer' (i.e. 'great warrior') in Hebrew. It can also be interpreted as "One who has a stump in place of a hand" or "One who cuts down".

gigi.e: Borrowed from French Gigi. Sometimes a pet form of English names such as Virginia or Genesis. Occasionally from initials G.G. (e.g. George General 'Gigi' Gryce).

giorgio.e: Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος.
giorgio.a: Giorgio is a male Italian given name derived from the Greek Georgios and sometimes a surname. It is equivalent to the English name George. Notable people with the name include:

giovanna.a: Giovanna is an Italian feminine first name. It is the feminine form of the masculine Giovanni, which is the Italian equivalent of John. As such, Giovanna corresponds to names like Joan, etc.

giovanni.a: Giovanni is a male Italian given name . It is the Italian equivalent of the English name John. Giovanni is frequently contracted to Gianni, Gian, or Gio, particularly in the name Gianbattista, and can also be found as a surname.

giulia.a: Giulia is the Italian version of the feminine given name Julia. The corresponding Italian male name is Giulio. People with that name include:

gloria.e: From Latin gloria (“glory”), first used as a name in 19th-century literature.
gloria.a: Gloria is the anglicized form of the Latin feminine given name gloriae , meaning immortal glory; glory, fame, renown, praise, honor. The name, as Maria de Gloria, was in regular use in Spain by 1700, one of a number of Titles of Mary in use for Portuguese and Spanish girls.

goldie.a: Goldie is a nickname or given name used in reference to an informal English diminutive word for gold or an English version of the Yiddish name Golda or Golde, also meaning gold. It was often used as a pet name for a girl with blonde hair.

grace.e: From the noun grace, first used by Puritans in the 16th century. In Roman Catholic use it may refer to Our Lady of Graces, cognate with Italian Grazia.
grace.a: Grace is a female name from the Latin gratia. It is often given in reference to the Christian concept of divine grace and used as a virtue name. As one of the theological virtues, Grace was in regular use by English Puritans in the 16th through the 18th centuries.

gracie.a: Gracie is a surname and a feminine given name, usually a diminutive form of Grace.

grainne.e: Possibly a derivative of Old Irish grán (“grain”) if originally the name of an agricultural goddess or a derivative of Middle Irish gráin (“awfulness, horror”) if the original sense was.
grainne.a: Gráinne is a feminine given name in the Irish language. The name is of an uncertain origin, although it is likely to be related to the word 'grá', which means 'love' in the Irish language.

grayson.a: Grayson is primarily a masculine given name. Notable people with the name include:

greyson.a: Greyson is a given name and a surname. Notable people with the name include:

gus.a: Gus is a masculine name, often a diminutive for Angus, August, Augustine/Augustin, Gustave, Constantine, Konstantinos, Augusten, Gustavo, Gusten, Augustus, Aengus, Argus, Fergus, Gustav, Gustafson, Ferguson, and Gussie.

gwen.e: A female given name. * Welsh Gwen. *. *.
gwen.a: Gwen is a Welsh feminine given name meaning "white, holy".
