hadi.a: Hadi or Hady is an Arabic masculine given name and surname, meaning "leader" or "guide". Al-Hadi ("The Guide") is one of the names of God in Islam. It is derived from the Arabic triconsonantal root ه د ي; also present in hidayah.

hadley.e: From Old English hǣþ (“heath”) + Old English leah (“woodland clearing”). Equivalent to heath + -leigh.
hadley.a: Hadley is a both a surname and a given name that is a transferred use of a place name of English origin that means “heather field.” The name has increased in popularity in recent years for girls in the United States and has ranked among the top 200 names used for American girls since 2011.

hafsa.a: Hafsa or Hafsah (Arabic: حفصة (often confused with Hafza and Hafiza, but all three of them are different names) is an Arabic female given name. It originated from Hafsa, the fourth wife of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and daughter of second Muslim caliph Umar.

haider.a: Haider is a South Asian and Arabic given name.

hailey.a: Hayley is an English given name. It is derived from the English surname Haley, which in turn was based on an Old English toponym, a compound of heg "hay" and leah "clearing or meadow". While it can be used for males, Hayley is most commonly a female given name.

hakeem.a: Hakeem is an Arabic-language given name, a romanization variant of Hakim. It is also used as a surname. Notable people with the name include:

halle.a: Halle is both a given name and a surname. Notable people with the name include:

hallie.a: Hallie is an English feminine given name that originated as a hypocorism for the name Harriet. Young children often have difficulty in pronouncing the letter r, which resulted in nicknames that substitute the letter l for r.

hamish.e: Anglicized spelling of Scottish Gaelic Sheumais, vocative case of Seumas, from English James (see for more). etc.
hamish.a: Hamish is an English and Scottish masculine given name, an Anglicized form of the vocative case of the Gaelic name Sheumais, itself the vocative of Seumas (the Gaelic equivalent of James).

hamza.e: From Arabic حَمْزَة, from the Arabic root.
hamza.a: Hamza is an Arabic masculine given name in the Muslim world. Meaning strong, and steadfast, it is an Arabic epithet for lion. It was borne by one of the Islamic prophet Muhammad's uncles, Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, a wrestler and an archer who was renowned for his strength and bravery in battle.

hamzah.a: Hamza is an Arabic masculine given name in the Muslim world. Meaning strong, and steadfast, it is an Arabic epithet for lion. It was borne by one of the Islamic prophet Muhammad's uncles, Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, a wrestler and an archer who was renowned for his strength and bravery in battle.

hana.a: Hana as a given name may have any of several origins. It is also a version of a Hebrew name from the root ḥ-n-n meaning "favour" or "grace", a Kurdish name meaning hope , a Persian name meaning flower and an Arabic name meaning "bliss" . As a Japanese name, it is usually translated as flower .

hanna.e: Variant spelling of Hannah or romanization of Hebrew חַנָּה, chiefly for the mother of Samuel, from חַנָּה (“grace, gracious, graced with child”). As an Oklahoman town, named for Hanna Bullett, one of the initial settlers.
hanna.a: Hanna, also spelled Hana, Hanah, or Chana, is a feminine given name of Hebrew origin.

hannah.e: From previous romanizations of Hebrew חַנָּה, chiefly for the mother of Samuel, from חַנָּה (“grace, gracious, graced with child”).
hannah.a: Hannah, also spelled Hanna, Hana, Hanah, or Chana, is a feminine given name of Hebrew origin . It is derived from the root ḥ-n-n, meaning "favour" or "grace". A Dictionary of First Names attributes the name to a word meaning 'He (God) has favoured me with a child'.

haris.a: Haris is a male Bosnian, Arabic and Greek unisex given name. The name "Haris" has two origins: Arabic and Greek. In Arabic, it is derived from the Arabic name Harith , which means "cultivator”.

harlan.e: American contraction of Harland, from Old English har (“grey”) / hara (“hare”) + land (“land”).
harlan.a: Harlan is a given name and a surname which may refer to:

harley.e: From Old English hær (“rock”) or hara (“hare”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to hare + -leigh.
harley.a: Harley is a unisex given name. The name is derived from the Old English words hara meaning hare, and lēah, meaning wood or clearing and meadow in later development of the language. The name Harley means "hare's meadow".

harlow.e: From Old English hær (“rock”) or here (“army”) + hlæw (“hill”).
harlow.a: Harlow is a given name of English origin, a transferred use of a surname and place name meaning "rock hill" or "army hill." Spelling variants Harlo and Harlowe are also in use. The name is associated with the actress Jean Harlow.

haroon.a: Harun , also transliterated as Haroon, Hamroun, or Haroun, is a masculine given name and surname of Arabic origin, related to the Hebrew name of the Prophet Aaron. Both are most likely of Egyptian origin, from ꜥḥꜣ rw, meaning "warrior lion". Notable people with the name include:

harper.a: Harper is an English, Scottish, and Irish surname that is also commonly used as a unisex given name in the United States. In some cases, the surname originated from an occupational name, and is derived from the Middle English harper, harpere ("harper").

harri.a: Harri is a given name and a surname. Notable people with these names include:

harriet.e: Anglicized form of French Henriette, feminine form of Henri (“Henry”), popular in England in the 18th and 19th centuries.
harriet.a: Harriet is a female given name. The name is an English version of the French Henriette, a female form of Henri. The male name Harry was formed in a similar way from Henry.

harris.e: From Harry + -s. From Harry, a male given name derived from a pronunciation of Old French Henri.
harris.a: Notable people with given name Harris include: Harris Allan (born 1985), Canadian actor and recording artist Harris Andrews (born 1996), Australian footballer with the Brisbane Lions Harris Armstrong , American modernist architect Harris Barron , American artist Harris Barton (born 1964), American…

harrison.a: Harrison is a common patronymic surname of Northern English origin. It means "son of Harry" or "Herry", due to the Middle English pronunciation of the given name Henry. It was first recorded in the 14th century.

harry.e: Medieval English spoken form of Old French Henri.
harry.a: Harry is a male given name. Beginning as a Middle English form of Henry, in the modern era it became a diminutive for several names beginning with "Har". The Norwegian term "harry" is derived from the name.

harun.a: Harun , also transliterated as Haroon, Hamroun, or Haroun, is a masculine given name and surname of Arabic origin, related to the Hebrew name of the Prophet Aaron. Both are most likely of Egyptian origin, from ꜥḥꜣ rw, meaning "warrior lion". Notable people with the name include:

harvey.e: From Haerviu, name of a Breton saint, from hoiarn (“iron”) + viu (“blazing”). Cognate with modern Breton Haerviu.
harvey.a: Harvey is an English and Scottish family and given name derived from the Old Breton personal name Huiarnviu (or Aeruiu), derived from the elements hoiarn, huiarn (modern Breton houarn) meaning "iron" and viu (Breton bev) meaning "blazing".

hasan.e: From Arabic حَسَن (“fine, good, good-looking, handsome, manly; strong”).
hasan.a: Hassan or Hasan is an Arabic masculine given name in the Muslim world. As a surname, Hassan may be Arabic, Irish, Scottish, or Jewish (Sephardic and Mizrahic) (see Hassan as a surname).

hashim.e: From Arabic هَاشِم (“Hashim”). The name signifies “breaker of bread”, from هَشَمَ (“to destroy, smash”).
hashim.a: Hashim is a common male Arabic given name.

hassan.e: From Arabic حَسَن (“fine, good, good-looking, handsome, manly; strong”).
hassan.a: Hassan or Hasan is an Arabic masculine given name in the Muslim world. As a surname, Hassan may be Arabic, Irish, Scottish, or Jewish (Sephardic and Mizrahic) (see Hassan as a surname).

hattie.a: Hattie or Hatty is traditionally an English feminine nickname for the name Harriet, long used, however, independently. It may refer to:

hawa.a: Hawa is a feminine given name. In Atayal, Hawa is a male given name. Hawa is the traditional Arabic, classical Hebrew and Swahili name for the Biblical and Qur'anic figure Eve.

hayden.e: Originally a place name, from Old English heg (“hay”) + denu (“valley”). Alternatively, from heiden (“heathen”).
hayden.a: Hayden is a given name in the English language. Its use as a first name comes from transferred use of the surname Hayden. Hayden was generally considered a masculine given name up until the mid-20th century.

hayley.e: Localities in England, from hēg (“hay”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to hay + -leigh.
hayley.a: Hayley is an English given name. It is derived from the English surname Haley, which in turn was based on an Old English toponym, a compound of heg "hay" and leah "clearing or meadow". While it can be used for males, Hayley is most commonly a female given name.

hazel.a: Hazel is a primarily female given name meaning "hazel", from the name of the tree or the color. It is derived from the Old English hæsel. It became a popular name in English-speaking countries during the 19th century, along with other names of plants or trees used for girls.

heath.e: English surname, from the noun heath.
heath.a: Heath is a masculine given name derived from the Old English word hǣþ, or heath. The name is a transferred use of the surname.

heather.e: From heather; the given name is one of the plant names taken up in the 19th century. The surname is habitational, also meaning someone living on a heath.
heather.a: Heather is an English primarily feminine given name. The botanical name refers to a variety of small shrubs with pink or white flowers which commonly grow in rocky areas. The brush is native to Scotland and England, but it is more commonly found in Scotland due to its rocky territories.

hector.e: From Latin Hectōr or Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ, from ἕκτωρ (“holding fast”), from ἔχω (“to have, hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“to hold; to overpower”).
hector.a: Hector () is an English, French, Scottish, and Spanish given name. The name is derived from the name of Hektor, a legendary Trojan champion who was killed by the Greek Achilles. The name Hektor is probably derived from the Greek ékhein, meaning "to have", "to hold", "to check", "restrain".

heidi.e: From Swiss German Heidi, a pet form of Adelheid, equivalent of English Adelaide and Alice. The name became internationally popular due to the children's book Heidi (1880).
heidi.a: Heidi is a Germanic feminine given name. It became an internationally popular first name as a direct result of the Swiss children's book, Heidi.

helen.e: From French Hélène, from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη.
helen.a: Helen is a feminine given name derived from the Ancient Greek name Ἑλένη, Helenē , which descends from Proto-Hellenic *Ηwelénā, from a pre-Hellenic or late Proto-Indo-European *Swelénā (a solar deity), ultimately derived from the Indo-European root *swel- (to shine, warm).

helena.e: A Latinate form of Helen, Latin Helena.
helena.a: Helena is a given name. It is the Latin form of Helen. Notable people with this name include:

henri.a: Henri ( ahn-REE) is the French form of the masculine given name Henry, also in Estonian, Finnish, German and Luxembourgish. Bearers of the given name include:

henrietta.e: Latinate form of French Henriette, derived from the male given name Henry.
henrietta.a: Henrietta is a feminine given name, derived from the male name Henry. The name is an English version of the French Henriette, a female form of Henri.

henry.e: From Middle English Henry, from () Henri, from *Haimrik, from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks. Cognate with German Heinrich, Dutch Hendrik, Hendrik, and Old Norse Heimríkr (Danish Henrik).
henry.a: Henry is a masculine given name derived from Old French Henri or Henry, which is derived from the Old Frankish name Heimeric, from Common Germanic “Haimarīks” (from *haima- "home" and *rīk- "ruler").

herbie.a: Herbie is a masculine given name, often a short form (hypocorism) of Herbert, and a nickname. It may refer to:

hettie.a: Hetty or Hettie is a female first name, often a diminutive form (hypocorism) of Henrietta. Another, less common spelling is Hetti. Hetty or Hetti may refer to:

holly.a: Holly is an English-language surname and given name. Holly is known as an English or Irish surname (variant Holley) it is either locational, ultimately derived from the Old English hol lēah "[dwelling by] the clearing by the hollow", or descriptive, from hol-ēage "hollow-eyed".

honey.a: Honey is an English hypocorism, independent given name, and surname meaning “honey”, which has long been used to sweeten foods and is a common English term of endearment. The word is derived from the Old English term hungi.

hope.a: Hope is a given name derived from the Middle English hope, ultimately from the Old English word hopian referring to a positive expectation or to the theological virtue of hope. It was used as a virtue name by the Puritans.

huda.a: Huda is a female name in Arabic, sometimes spelled as Houda or Hoda which means "right guidance". Notable people with the name include:

hudson.a: Hudson is an English masculine given name which originated from the surname Hudson.

hugh.e: From the aristocratic and saint's name Hughe, brought to England by Normans, from a short form of names beginning with Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“heart, mind”), such as Hubert. Cognate with Old English hyġe (“mind, spirit, intellect”).
hugh.a: Hugh is the English-language variant of the masculine given name Hugues, itself the Old French variant of Hugo, a short form of Continental Germanic given names beginning in the element *hug- "mind, spirit" (Old English hyġe).

hughie.e: From Hugh + ie. Regarding rain, various etymologies have been proposed; see Send 'er down, Hughie!.
hughie.a: Hughie is a masculine given name and nickname (usually of the given name Hugh). People named Hughie include:

hugo.e: From Old French Hugo, of origin, from *hugi (“thought, mind, spirit”).
hugo.a: Hugo is a surname and a masculine given name of German origin. The English version of the name is Hugh, the Italian version is Ugo. The name Hugo is actually a short form of old names like Hugbert and Hugbald.

humaira.e: Arabic حُمَيْرة, diminutive of حُمْرة (“redness”), or from حُمَيْرَاة.
humaira.a: Humaira is a Muslim female name of Arabic origin.

hunter.a: Hunter is an English unisex given name. Notable people with the name include:

huxley.e: From the personal name *Hucc + -s- + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”). The first element could also be husc (“insult, scorn, mockery”).

ian.a: Ian is a male name of English, Scottish Gaelic and Hebrew origin, which is derived from the Hebrew given name יוֹחָנָן and corresponds to the English name John. The spelling is an Anglicization of the Scottish Gaelic forename Iain.

iarla.a: Iarla is a masculine given name. Notable people with the name include: Iarla Ó Lionáird (born 1963 or 1964), Irish singer and record producer Iarla Tannian (born 1984), Irish hurler centre back

ibrahim.a: Ibrahim is the Arabic name of Abraham, the common Hebrew patriarch of the Abrahamic religions, including Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

ida.e: Short form of obsolete names beginning with Germanic īd "work", used for both sexes in medieval England. It was revived in the 19th century, partly mistaken for a Greek name, for the Mount Ida of classical mythology.
ida.a: Ida is a feminine given name found in Europe and North America. It is popular in Scandinavian countries, where it is pronounced Ee-da. The name has an ancient Germanic etymology, according to which it means ‘industrious’ or ‘prosperous’.

idrees.a: Idris is both a Welsh and an Arabic given name (usually masculine), also given as surname; the Welsh and Arabic names are not related and have two different etymologies. Welsh: 'Ardent lord', from udd (lord, prince) + ris (ardent, enthusiastic, impulsive).

idris.a: Idris is both a Welsh and an Arabic given name (usually masculine), also given as surname; the Welsh and Arabic names are not related and have two different etymologies. Welsh: 'Ardent lord', from udd (lord, prince) + ris (ardent, enthusiastic, impulsive).

ignacy.a: Ignacy is a Polish given name, equivalent of the name Ignatius.

ilinca.a: Ilinca is a Romanian given name. It is related to the names Elena and Ileana.

ilyas.a: Ilyas is a form of the masculine given name Elias or Elijah.

iman.a: Iman is a given name found in many cultures, that can be both masculine and feminine. Variations of spelling include Eman, Emon, and Imaan. In Islamic cultures, the name Iman (variously spelled Eman, Imaan, Imane) comes from the Arabic word meaning 'faith' or 'belief'.

imani.e: Borrowed, from imani (“faith, belief”), from Arabic إِيمَان.

imogen.e: First used by William Shakespeare in Cymbeline, a misprint for Innogen, from Scottish Gaelic inghean (“girl, maiden”)
imogen.a: Imogen (), or Imogene (), is a feminine given name; see Innogen § Name for its origins.

imran.a: Imran, Imraan, Emraan, or Emran is a masculine given name and surname of Arabic origin. The name Imran is found in the Quranic chapter called Family of ʿImrān . Notable people with the name include:

india.e: Old English India, Indea, from Latin India, from Ancient Greek Ἰνδία, from Ancient Greek Ἰνδός (“Indus river”), from Sanskrit सिन्धु, ultimately from *síndʰuš (“river”).
india.a: India is a feminine given name derived from the name of the country India, which itself takes its name from the Indus River. The name was used for India Wilkes, a character in the novel and film Gone with the Wind.

indiana.e: From Indian + a. From Indiana Territory, dating from 1800, noting the territory's large Native American Indian population. From Indian Territory.

indigo.a: Indigo is a given name often used in reference to the color, a shade between the colors blue and violet. Deep blue indigo dye was originally derived from the plant called true indigo. The name is in use for both boys and girls in the Anglosphere.

ines.a: Ines, and variants, is a feminine given name related to Agnes. Used alone it may refer to: Saint Ines , virgin–martyr, saint Ines (Eda-Ines Etti; born 1981), Estonian singer

ioan.a: Ioan is a variation on the name John found in Aromanian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Russian, Welsh , and Sardinian. It is usually masculine. The female equivalent in Romanian and Bulgarian is Ioana.

iona.e: Probably a misreading of Latin Ioua, an attempt to Latinize Old Irish Í.
iona.a: Iona is a given name that is taken from the Scottish island of Iona, which has a particular significance in the history of Christianity. The derivation of this island name itself is uncertain. The earliest forms of the name enabled toponymist William J.

iqra.a: Iqra is a feminine given name of Arabic origin. Notable people with the name include:

irene.e: Borrowed from French Irène, from Ancient Greek Εἰρήνη (“peace”), name of a goddess of peace, of early Christian saints, and of an 8th-century Byzantine empress.

iris.a: Iris is a feminine name. The name came into use in English-speaking countries in the 1500s, first in reference to the goddess, and was later used along with other Ancient Greek names revived by 17th-century British poets, such as Doris and Phyllis.

isaac.e: From Middle English Ysaac, from Latin Isaac, from Ancient Greek Ἰσαάκ, from Hebrew יצחק. Explained in Genesis as referring to his mother Sarah’s laughing when she was told she would have a son at her old age.
isaac.a: Isaac transliterated from Yitzhak, Yitzchok is a given name derived from Judaism and a given name among Jewish, Christian, and Muslim societies, generally in reference to the above. "Ike" and "Ise" are also short forms of the name.

isabel.e: From Spanish Isabel, from Elisabel, from Latin Elisabeth, from Ancient Greek Ἐλισάβετ, from Hebrew אֱלִישֶׁבַע (“my God is an oath”).
isabel.a: Isabel is a female name of Spanish origin. It originates as the medieval Spanish form of Elisabeth. Arising in the 12th century, it became popular in England in the 13th century following the marriage of Isabella of Angoulême to the king of England.

isabella.e: Latinate and Italian form of Isabel. The grape cultivar is popularly thought to have been discovered by a Mrs Isabella Gibbs of South Carolina in 1816.
isabella.a: Isabella or Isabela is a feminine given name, the Latinate and Italian form of Isabel, the Spanish form Isabelle, the French form, and Isobel, the Scottish form of the name Elizabeth. All are ultimately derived from the Hebrew Elisheba.

isabelle.a: Isabel is a female name of Spanish origin. It originates as the medieval Spanish form of Elisabeth. Arising in the 12th century, it became popular in England in the 13th century following the marriage of Isabella of Angoulême to the king of England.

isaiah.e: From Ancient Greek Ἠσαΐας from Hebrew יְשַׁעְיָהוּ.
isaiah.a: Isaiah is a masculine name of biblical origin. It comes from the Hebrew: יְשַׁעְיָהוּ , meaning 'Yahweh is salvation'. The best known Isaiah is a prophet, in the Book of Isaiah.

ishaan.e: From Sanskrit ईशान (“Ishana”), a Hindu deity and guardian of the northeast direction.
ishaan.a: Ishaan is a given name of Indian origin.

ishaq.a: Ishak, Ishaq, Isak, Isaque, Isaac, Isaak, Isaach or Eshaq is a masculine given name (first name), the Arabic form of Isaac. Ishak (Isaac) was the son of Ibrahim (Abraham) and Sarah, patriarchs in the Bible and the Quran.

isla.a: Isla is a feminine given name traditionally of primarily Scottish usage, derived from "Islay", which is the name of an island off the west coast of Scotland. It is also the name of two Scottish rivers. The root word has no known origin.

ismael.a: Ismael is a masculine given name of Arabic origin. Notable people with the name include:

ismail.a: Ismail, Esmael, Esmaeel, Esmail, İsmail, or Ismaïl is a masculine given name of Arabic origin. It corresponds to the English name Ishmael. Notable people with the name include:

isobel.a: Isobel is the Scottish form of the female given name Isabel. It originates from the medieval form of the name Elisabeth.

israel.e: From Middle English Israel, borrowed from Latin Israel, from Ancient Greek Ἰσραήλ, from Hebrew יִשְׂרָאֵל (“Israel”). In the Bible, it is said to be from the name יִשְׂרֶה אֵל given to Jacob in, after which his descendants came to be known…
israel.a: Israel is a masculine Hebrew name.

issa.a: Issa is a given name that means Jesus in Arabic. It may refer to: Christ in Islam El-Issa family

issac.a: Isaac transliterated from Yitzhak, Yitzchok is a given name derived from Judaism and a given name among Jewish, Christian, and Muslim societies, generally in reference to the above. "Ike" and "Ise" are also short forms of the name.

ivan.e: From Russian Ива́н, and from Ivan in several languages. and its relatives, etc.
ivan.a: Ivan is a male given name of Slavic and Hebrew origin, related to a variant of the Greek name Iōánnēs (English: John), which in turn derives from the Hebrew יוֹחָנָן , meaning "God is gracious". The name is strongly associated with Slavic countries and cultures.

ivar.a: Ivar (Old Norse Ívarr) is a Scandinavian masculine given name. Another variant of the name is Iver, which is more common in Norway. The Old Norse name has several possible etymologies.

ivie.a: Ivie is a given name and surname. Notable people with the name include:

ivo.e: Latinate form of a medieval name of origin, from Proto-Germanic *īhwaz (“yew, bow”). Name of French and English saints. Cognate with modern French Yves.
ivo.a: Ivo is a masculine given name, in use in various European languages. The name used in western European languages originates as a Germanic name.

ivor.e: Medieval form of Old Norse Ívarr.
ivor.a: Ivor is an English masculine given name derived either directly from Norse Ívarr, or through Welsh (which spells it Ifor) or Irish and Scottish Gaelic (which spell it Íomhar), all of which likely derive it also from the original Norse form.

ivy.e: From ivy, the name of a plant. An ivy branch used to be hung outside an establishment to advertise that it sold alcohol, so it may originally been an occupationational surname for the proprietor of such an establishment.
ivy.a: Ivy is a given name or surname taken from the name of the plant. It became popular as a given name in the late 1800s, along with other plant and flower names for girls.

izabella.e: Either from Spanish Isabel or Hebrew אִיזֶבֶל (Jezebel).
izabella.a: Izabella is a Polish feminine given name.

izzy.e: From the root of the names + -y. The common noun derives from Isaac and Israel, male given names of Hebrew origin, popular among Jewish people, the latter also being the name of the self-defined Jewish state.

jace.a: Jace or Jase is a masculine given name. It is often short for Jason. It is also, less commonly, a surname.

jack.e: From Middle English Jak, Jakke (also Jackin, Jankyn, etc.), from Anglo-Norman Jakke, *Janke, from Janke, diminutive of Jan (“John”); equivalent to John + -kin.
jack.a: Jack is a given name of English origin. In modern usage, Jack is often a given name on its own, although it can be used as a diminutive of other given names. Since the late 20th century, Jack has become one of the most common names for boys in many English-speaking countries.

jackson.a: Jackson is an English masculine given name that originated as a transferred use of the surname, which means "son of Jack". It is in regular use, along with spelling variants such as Jaxon, and Jacksen, Jacson, and Jaxson.

jacob.e: From Middle English Iacob, from Iācōbus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος, from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב, from the third-person singular masculine imperfective form of the Semitic verb "to heel" (with various meanings), in turn from עָקֵב (“heel…
jacob.a: Jacob is a common masculine given name of Hebrew origin. The English form is derived from the Latin Iacobus, from the Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iakobos), ultimately from the Hebrew יַעֲקֹב , the name of Jacob, biblical patriarch of the Israelites, and a major figure in the Abrahamic religions.

jacques.o: French < Latin < Ancient Greek < Biblical Hebrew
jacques.a: The name Jacques, derived from Jacob, is believed to have originated in the northwest Brittany region of France in the Middle Ages, and occurs in variations, such as Jacq, as both a given name and a surname.

jade.e: From the precious stone jade; taken into general use in the 1970s.
jade.a: Jade is a given name derived from the ornamental stone jade, which is used in artwork and in jewellery-making. The name is derived from the Spanish piedra de la ijada, which means "stone of the bowels". There was a belief that when jade was placed on the stomach, it could cure colic in babies.

jaden.a: Jaden is a unisex given name with roots in Hebrew, meaning "God has heard." It is also found as a surname. Notable people with the name "Jaden" include:

jadon.a: Jadon is a Hebrew given name meaning "God has heard", "thankful" (according to Strong's Concordance), "a judge", or "whom God has judged" and the name of two characters in Biblical history.

jaiden.a: Jayden, Jadin, Jadyn, Jaiden, and Jaden (among other variations) are unisex given names.

jake.e: Originally a medieval variant of Jack; today also used as a diminutive form of Jacob and James.
jake.a: Jake is a masculine given name derived from Jacob. It can also be a nickname of Jacob and various other given names.

jakob.a: Jakob is a masculine given name that is a variant spelling of the Hebrew given name Jacob.

jakub.e: Latin Iacōbus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος, from Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (“Jacob”), from עָקֵב (“heel of the foot”).
jakub.a: Jakub is a masculine given name. It is the Polish, Belarusian, Czech, Slovak and Bosnian form of the name Jacob. In Polish and Czech, the diminutive form of Jakub is Kuba.

jamal.a: Jamaal, Jamal, Jammal, or variants is an Arabic given name and surname meaning "beauty." It is popular in the Arab and Muslim worlds and among African Americans. Though its usage is typically as a masculine name, it has been used as a given name for women.

james.e: The English New Testament form of Jacob, from Middle English James, from Old French James, from Iācōmus, spoken and altered pronunciation of Latin Iācōbus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος, from Ἰακώβ, from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב, from the…
james.a: James is an English language given name that is a derivative of the name Jacob, most commonly used for males.

jamie.a: Jamie is a unisex name. Traditionally a masculine name, it can be diminutive form of James or, more rarely, other names and is of Scots language origin. It is also given as a name in its own right.

jana.e: From Jana, ultimately from Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה, the feminized form of יְהוֹחָנָן which produced John and its many doublets. As a placeholder name, cf. similar use of John and Jack and earlier use of Joan in the same role.

jane.e: Variant of Jeanne, from French Jeanne, from Middle French Jehanne, from Johanna, variant of Latin Ioanna under influence from Latin Iōhannēs, from Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה, the feminized form of יְהוֹחָנָן which produced John and its…
jane.a: Jane is a feminine given name.

janelle.a: Janelle, and variations such as Janegel, are feminine given names, variant of Jane which derives from the Greek name Ἰωάννης (Iōannēs), derived from the Hebrew name יוֹחָנָן (Yochanan), meaning "God is merciful".

jarlath.a: Jarlath is an Irish given name.

jasmine.e: From French jasmin, from Arabic يَاسَمِين, from یاسمین, from earlier یاسمن, from yʾsmn'.
jasmine.a: Jasmine is a feminine given name.

jason.e: From the Ancient Greek Ἰάσων, from ἰάομαι (“I heal”). The Jason mentioned in the New Testament (Acts 17:5-9, Romans 16:21) is probably a Greek rendering of Joshua.
jason.a: Jason is a common masculine given name.

jasper.e: A name given to one of the Magi in a medieval European cult, from Biblical Hebrew גִּזְבָּר, ultimately from *ganǰabarah; see it for more.
jasper.a: Jasper is a masculine given name of Persian origin, meaning "treasurer". The etymology of the given name Jasper (of Persian origin) is unrelated to that of the gemstone jasper (of Semitic origin). Jasper may refer to:

jax.e: Shortened from Jackson, Jaxon or fanciful spelling of the surname Jacks.

jaxon.a: Jaxon or Jaxxon is a given name and surname. Notable people with the name include:

jaxson.a: Jaxson is a given name. It is a variant spelling of the given name Jackson.

jay.a: Jay (or Jai) is a predominantly male given name. 'Jaya' is a female variation or female given name with same meaning and origin from Sanskrit. It has multiple origins and meanings, commonly associated with intelligence, cheerfulness, and victory.

jayce.a: Jayce is a first name that is often an abbreviation of Jason. Notable people and fictional characters with the name include:

jayden.e: Invented at the end of the 20th century by American parents who wanted to combine the initial "J" with the fashionable sound of Aidan, Braden, Caden and Hayden.
jayden.a: Jayden, Jadin, Jadyn, Jaiden, and Jaden (among other variations) are unisex given names.

jemima.e: From the name of a minor biblical character, from Hebrew יְמִימָה (“dove”). By folk etymology also used as a feminine form of James.
jemima.a: Jemima or Jemimah is a feminine given name of Hebrew origin meaning 'dove'. It may refer to:

jennifer.e: From Cornish Gweniver, from Gwynnever (cognate with Welsh Gwenhwyfar), from *Gwɨnnohuɨβar. Compare Irish Fionnabhair, which may be cognate.
jennifer.a: Jennifer, also spelled Jenifer or Jenefer, is a feminine given name, the Cornish form of Guinevere, that became popular in the English-speaking world in the 20th century.

jensen.a: Jensen is a unisex given name. Notable people with the given name include:

jenson.a: Jenson is an patronymic surname meaning "son of Jen", where Jen is a short form of Old French Jehan i.e. John. It may also be an Americanized form of the surnames Jensen or Jenssen.

jeremiah.e: Latin Jeremias, from Ancient Greek Ἰερεμίας, from Hebrew יִרְמְיָה (“Jeremiah”).
jeremiah.a: Jeremiah is a male given name meaning "Yahweh loosens", or "Yahweh will raise", or "God is high", and having its origin in ancient Hebrew. Jeremias is a form that it takes in some Romance languages.

jeremy.a: Jeremy () is an English-language male given name, deriving from various translations and interpretations as anglicized and diminutive form of the given name Jeremiah.

jesse.e: From Ancient Greek Ἰεσσαί, from Hebrew יִשַׁי.
jesse.a: Jesse is a given name of Hebrew origin. It derives its popularity from the biblical figure Jesse, father of Israelite monarch David. The English version is derived from the Latin Iesse, borrowed from the Ancient Greek Iessaí , and ultimately from the Hebrew Yišay .

jessica.e: First used by William Shakespeare in Merchant of Venice in the early 17th century, probably from Hebrew יִסְכָּה, a proper name meaning "he will see/behold/look for", the 3ms imperfect form of a verb ultimately, itself an alternative form…
jessica.a: Jessica (originally Iessica, also Jesica, Jesika, Jessicah, Jessika, or Jessikah) is a female given name of English origin. The oldest written record of the name with its current spelling is found as the name of the Shakespearean character Jessica, from the play The Merchant of Venice.

jessie.a: Jessie is a given name in its own right, but may also be a nickname for the given name Jessica. It is generally considered the feminine form of Jesse. The name Jess is also a given name.

jimmy.a: Jimmy is a masculine given name. It is often used as a diminutive form of the given name James, along with its short form, Jim.

joanna.e: From Latin Joanna, from Ἰωάννα, from Hebrew יוֹחָנָה, the feminized form of יְהוֹחָנָן which produced John and its many doublets.
joanna.a: Joanna is a feminine given name deriving from Koine Greek: Ἰωάννα, romanized: Iōanna from Hebrew: יוֹחָנָּה, romanized: Yôḥānnāh, lit. 'God is gracious'. Variants in English include Joan, Joann, Joanne, and Johanna. Other forms of the name in English are Jan, Jane, Janet, Janice, Jean, and Jeanne.

joe.a: Joe is a masculine given name, usually a short form of Joseph.

joel.e: Principally from Medieval Latin Joel, from Late Latin Ioel, from Ἰωήλ, from Biblical Hebrew יוֹאֵל (“Yah God”). Also partially from and variants of Breton Judicaël, also related to Joyce and Jocelyn. Cf. Elijah.
joel.a: Joel or Yoel is a male name derived from יוֹאֵל Standard Hebrew, Yoʾel, Tiberian Hebrew, or Yôʾēl, meaning "Yahu is El" (El being a Northwest Semitic word meaning 'god' or 'deity'), "YHWH is God", or the modern translation "Yahweh is God". A pious Jew would never use the word "Yahweh".

joey.a: Joey is a unisex given name or nickname, more commonly used for males. It can be a diminutive of names that begin with J, most commonly Joseph, Joshua, Joe, Josephine and Johanna.

john.e: From Middle English John, Johan, Johannes, from Anglo-Norman Jehan, Johan, and also Old English Iohannes, both from Iōhannēs, variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Ἰωάννης, from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן, perhaps contracted from a former…
john.a: John ( JON) is a very common given male name in the English language, ultimately of Hebrew origin. Traditionally in the Anglosphere, it was the most common, although it has not been since the latter half of the 20th century.

johnny.e: From John + y. In the sense of an Englishman, compare John Bull.
johnny.a: Johnny is an English language personal name. It is often a nickname, but from the 16th century it has sometimes been a given name in its own right for males and, less commonly, females. Variant forms of Johnny include Johnnie, Johnney, Johhny, Johnni and Johni.

jonah.a: Jonah is a masculine given name derived from the Hebrew: יוֹנָה, Yonā, meaning dove or pigeon. It is the name of the Abrahamic prophet Jonah.

jonas.e: From Latin Iōnās, from Ἰωνᾶς, from Biblical Hebrew יוֹנָה (“dove”).
jonas.a: Jonas is a common male name in many countries in the Western world and Northeast Africa. It is primarily used as a first name, but also occurs as a surname. It is particularly frequent in Germany, Israel, Ethiopia, the Netherlands, Flanders and Scandinavia.

jonathan.e: Hebrew יְהוֹנָתָן, יוֹנָתָן, apparently with influence.

joni.e: Commonly used as a diminutive of Joan.
joni.a: Joni is a unisex given name.

jordan.e: From Latin Iordanēs, from Ancient Greek Ἰορδάνης, from Biblical Hebrew יַרְדֵּן (“Jordan (river)”).
jordan.a: Jordan is a given name. The form found in Western names originates from Hebrew: ירדן, romanized: Yarden, relating to the Jordan River in West Asia.

joseph.e: From Middle English Ioseph, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יוֹסֵף; a son of Jacob. is a reference to the story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife in Genesis 39.
joseph.a: Joseph is a common male name, derived from the Hebrew Yosef . "Joseph" is used, along with "Josef", mostly in English, French and partially German languages. This spelling is also found as a variant in the languages of the modern-day Nordic countries. In Portuguese and Spanish, the name is "José".

josephine.e: From French Joséphine, diminutive of Josèphe, feminine form of Joseph. Popularized in English by Josephine Bonaparte, the empress of Napoleonic France.
josephine.a: Josephine is a female name. It is the English version of the French name Joséphine, itself a female variant of the name Joseph , which is ultimately derived from the Hebrew name Yosef , meaning "he shall add/grow".

josh.a: Josh is a masculine given name. It is frequently a diminutive (hypocorism) of the given name Joshua and historically a diminutive of Josiah but has been used independently as a given name. The diminutive has been in use since the 19th century.

joshua.e: From Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, perhaps from הוֹשֵׁעַ with addition of יהוה (“Yahweh”), thus meaning "Yahweh is salvation". See הוֹשִׁיעַ (“to save”).
joshua.a: Joshua is a given name derived from the Hebrew יְהוֹשֻׁעַ , prominently belonging the early Hebrew leader of the Exodus period Joshua, who has a major role in several books of the Bible.

josiah.a: Josiah () is a masculine given name derived from the Hebrew Yoshi-yahu (Hebrew: יֹאשִׁיָּהוּ, Modern: Yošiyyáhu, Tiberian: Yôšiyyāhû, "Yahweh has healed". Josiah was a King of Judah in the Bible. The Latin form Josias was used in some early English translations of the Bible.

josie.a: Josie ( or ) is a given name that is often a diminutive of the female given name Josephine.

jovan.a: Jovan is a Serbian male given name equivalent to English "John" or Slavic "Ivan", from Hebrew: יהוחנן. The name is common amongst Orthodox Christians as a result of John the Baptist (Sveti Jovan Krstitelj)

joy.e: From the noun joy, first used by Puritans in the 17th century.
joy.a: Joy is a common unisex given name. Among Saint Thomas Christians in Kerala it is a shorten form for Joseph, Ouseph or Jose. A common variant of the name is the other female given name Joyce (name).

judah.a: Judah is a masculine given name of Hebrew origin. It is the English form of Yehudah , the Hebrew name of the biblical figure Judah, founder of the Tribe of Judah and thus, the eponym of the Kingdom of Judah and the Jews.

jude.e: Short form of Judas, used in an attempt to distinguish the Apostle Judas Thaddaeus from Judas Iscariot. From Old Testament Judah, Hebrew יְהוּדָה, said to mean “praised”.
jude.a: Jude is an English unisex, primarily masculine given name. It is ultimately derived from the Hebrew name יְהוּדָה, which can be transliterated as Yehuḏa, means "praise", and whose short form was more directly adopted into English as Judah.

julia.e: From Latin Iūlia, feminine form of the Roman gens name Iūlius. Further popularized by early Christian saints.
julia.a: Julia is a feminine given name. It is a Latinate feminine form of the name Julio and Julius. (For further details on etymology, see the Wiktionary entry "Julius.") The given name Julia had been in use throughout Late Antiquity (e.g.

julian.a: Julian is a common male given name in the United States, Germany, Austria, the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Netherlands (as Juliaan), France (as Julien), Italy (as Giuliano), Russia [Iulian (Yulian)] Spain, Latin America (as Julián in Spanish and Juliano or Julião in Portuguese), Iulian in Romanian…

juliet.e: Italian Giulietta, diminutive of Giulia, from Latin Iūlia, feminine of Iūlius, a Roman family name. Cognate with French Juliette.
juliet.a: Juliet is a feminine given name, an English form of the Italian Giulietta, which is a diminutive form of Italian Giulia. It is also an English form of the French Juliette, which is a diminutive form of the French Julie.

juliette.a: Juliette is a feminine personal name of French origin. It is a diminutive of Julie.

june.e: From Middle English June, june, re-Latinised variants of earlier Middle English Juyn, juyng, from Old French juing, juin, from Latin iūnius, the month of the goddess Iuno (“Juno”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéwHō, from…
june.a: June is a gender-neutral given name. It is a common feminine name and a less common masculine name in English-speaking countries. It comes from the name of the month, which is derived from Juno, the name of a Roman goddess of youth and protection.

junior.a: Junior is a given name, nickname, and surname often used by people who are the second in their family with the same name (for more information, see generational titles). It may refer to:

juniper.e: A topographic surname from juniper. In some cases matronymic from an equivalent of Jennifer influenced by folk etymology.
juniper.a: Juniper is a given name used either in reference to the English common name for the juniper tree or berry, or in reference to a derivation of the Welsh name Guinevere. Juniper has historically been used as both a boys' name and a girls' name.

juno.e: From Middle English Juno, from Latin Iūnō of uncertain origin. One hypothesis is derivation from Proto-Indo-European *dyúh₃onh₂- (“she of heavenly authority”), from *dyew- (“sky, heaven”) + *-Hō (“burden, authority”), reflecting her role…

justin.e: Name of early saints, Latin Iūstīnus, from Iūstus + -īnus, from iūstus (“just”).
justin.a: Justin is a masculine given name of Latin origin. It is the anglicized form of the Latin given name Justinus, a derivative of Justus, meaning "just", "fair", or "righteous". Justinus was the name borne by various early saints, notably a 2nd-century Christian apologist and a 3rd-century martyr.

kacper.a: Kacper is a predominantly Polish masculine given name, a variant of Caspar.

kaden.a: Kaden is a given name, a variant spelling of Caden, as well as a surname.

kai.e: Taken into regular use in the 1990s, with earlier popularity peaks in Scandinavia and Germany. The medieval Danish Kaj is possibly of Roman origin, Latinized as Caius, like the rare medieval English male given name Kay.
kai.a: The name Kai has various origins and meanings in different cultures: In Estonian, Kai is a female name derived from Katherine. In Persian, Kai, or Kay, is a male name, meaning "king". It is also the name of a mythological shah (king) in the Shahnameh.

kaleb.e: From Hebrew כלב (“dog”), possibly referring to a dog’s unconditional devotion to its master.
kaleb.a: Kaleb is a masculine given name, a variant spelling of Caleb, as well as a surname.

kali.a: Kali is an Indian given name and surname of Sanskrit origins from the name Kālá. Notable people with this name include the following:

kane.a: The given name Kane is shared by:

kara.a: Kara is both a given name and a surname with various, unrelated origins in various cultures. As an English name, it is usually considered a modern spelling variant of the Italian endearment cara, meaning beloved, or the Irish word cara, meaning friend.

karam.a: Karam is a given name and a surname of Arabic origin. People with the name include:

kareem.a: Kareem or Karim is a masculine given name and surname of Arabic origin that means "generous", "noble", or "honourable"; it is also one of the Names of God in Islam. The feminine form is Karima. Notable people with the name include:

karim.a: Kareem or Karim is a masculine given name and surname of Arabic origin that means "generous", "noble", or "honourable"; it is also one of the Names of God in Islam. The feminine form is Karima. Notable people with the name include:

karina.a: Karina is a female given name. In modern times, the country where it is most used (in absolute terms) is Russia, whereas Belarus is where it is the most popular (relating to its population). It is a short form of Katarina – which in turn shares the same origin as its English form, Katherine.

kasper.a: Kasper is a masculine given name which may refer to: Kasper Andersen (cyclist) (born 2002), Danish cyclist Kasper Andersen (speedway rider) (born 1998), Danish speedway rider Kasper Irming Andersen (born 1986), Danish handball player Kasper Bøgelund (born 1980), Danish retired footballer Kasper…

kate.a: Kate is a feminine given name. It is often a short form of Katherine, Caitlin, and other names.

katherine.a: Katherine (), also spelled Catherine and other variations, is a feminine given name. The name and its variants are popular in countries where large Christian populations exist, because of its associations with the early Christian saint Catherine of Alexandria.

kathleen.e: Anglicization of Caitlín, an equivalent of the English Catherine.
kathleen.a: Kathleen is a female given name, used in English- and Irish-language communities. Sometimes spelled Cathleen, it is an Anglicized form of Caitlín, the Irish form of Cateline, which was the Old French form of Catherine.

katie.a: Katie is an English feminine name. It is a form of Katherine, Kate, Caitlin, Kathleen, Katey and their related forms. It is frequently used on its own.

kaya.a: Kaya is a given name most commonly found in Turkey and Japan.

kayden.a: Caden is a given name in English-speaking countries that is most commonly used for males. It rose in popularity in the early 2000s due to the popularity of similar-sounding names, such as Aidan, Braden, Hayden, and Jadon.

kayla.e: A modern invention possibly based on Kay or Michaela; possibly formed on the pattern of Layla.
kayla.a: Kayla is a recently created English feminine given name combining the name elements Kay and -la. Its use has been influenced by similar-sounding names such as Kaylee.

kayleigh.a: Kayleigh is a feminine given name.

kealan.a: Caolán is a masculine given name of Irish origin, derived from the Irish word "caol-" ("slender, narrow [and] fine"). The name has a number of Anglicisations, including "Kelan", "Keelan" and "Kealan". Notable people with the name Caolán, Kelan, and Keelan include:

keegan.a: Keegan is an Anglicisation of the Irish clan name Mac Aodhagáin, now often used as a forename. The name means "son (or descendant) of Aodhagán" . In North America the name is most often given to boys, but has gradually become unisex.

keelan.a: Caolán is a masculine given name of Irish origin, derived from the Irish word "caol-" ("slender, narrow [and] fine"). The name has a number of Anglicisations, including "Kelan", "Keelan" and "Kealan". Notable people with the name Caolán, Kelan, and Keelan include:

keelin.a: Keelin is a given name. Notable people with the given name include: Keelin Fox, Irish badminton player Keelin Godsey (born 1984), American transgender hammer thrower Keelin Shanley (born 1968), Irish journalist, newsreader and presenter Keelin Winters (born 1988), American soccer player

keeva.a: Caoimhe , sometimes anglicised as Keeva, is an Irish feminine given name derived from Irish caomh 'dear; precious, beloved; belonging to the family'. It is derived from the same root as the masculine name Caoimhín (Kevin).

keira.e: A modern feminine form of Kieran, from Irish ciar (“black, dark, little dark one”).
keira.a: Keira is a feminine given name. It is an Anglicized version of the given name Ciara and means "little dark one". It is associated with Irish or English heritage.

kellan.a: Kellan, also spelt Kellin, is a male given name. Similar names include Kellen, Kaelan, Kallen, Kelan, and Kellyn.

kelly.a: Kelly is a unisex given name derived from an Anglicized version of the Irish masculine name Ceallach or a transferred use of the Irish surname O'Ceallaigh. O'Ceallaigh, which means "descendant of Ceallach", was Anglicized as Kelly or O'Kelly; the meaning of the personal name Ceallach is uncertain.

kendall.e: From the placename Kendal in Cumbria, "valley of the river Kent", and Kendale in Humberside, from Old Norse kelda (“spring”) + dalr (“valley”).
kendall.a: Kendall is a unisex given name. Notable people and characters with the name include:

kendrick.a: Kendrick is a surname, sometimes used as a masculine given name, which may originate from: The Welsh name Cynwrig meaning "greatest champion", or The Anglo-Saxon name Cyneric meaning cyne (royal, of a king) + rīks (king, ruler).

kennedy.e: Irish Ó Cinnéidigh (ceann + éidigh) or Scottish Gaelic Ceannaideach (ceann + aideach. Compare Kenneth and Irish eitigh (“refuse, reject”).
kennedy.a: Kennedy (also spelled Kenedi, Kennedie, Kennedi) () is a unisex given name in the English language. The name is an Anglicised form of a masculine given name in the Irish language.

kenneth.e: Anglicized form of two names, Old Irish Cináed, the name of Scottish kings derived, and the saint's name Cainnech (modern Scottish Gaelic Coinneach), as in the surname Mackenzie.
kenneth.a: Kenneth is a given name of Gaelic origin. The name is an Anglicised form of two entirely different Gaelic personal names: Cainnech and Cináed. The modern Scottish Gaelic form of Cainnech is Coinneach; the name was derived from a byname meaning "handsome", "comely".

kenny.a: Kenny is a surname, a given name, and a diminutive of several different given names. In Ireland, the surname is an Anglicisation of the Irish Ó Cionnaith, also spelt Ó Cionnaoith and Ó Cionaodha, meaning "descendant of Cionnaith".

kerrie.a: Kerrie is a feminine given name. Notable people with the name include:

kerry.a: Kerry or Kerri is a unisex English language given name of Gaelic origin. In its original form Ciarraighe (Ciarraí), it denoted the kingdom of Ciar (ciar raighe), Ciar being the son of Fergus mac Róich, who gave his name to County Kerry.

kevin.e: Name of a seventh-century Irish saint, from Irish Caoimhghin or Caoimhín, from Old Irish Cóemgen. It first became popular outside Ireland in the mid-twentieth century.
kevin.a: Kevin is the anglicized form of the Irish masculine given name Caoimhín . It is composed of caomh "dear; noble"; Old Irish cóem and -gin . The variant Kevan is anglicised from Caoimheán, an Irish diminutive form.

khadija.a: Khadija, Khadijah, Khadeeja, Khatija, or Khatijah is a feminine given name of Arabic origin. It is the name of Khadija bint Khuwaylid, the first wife of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

khadijah.a: Khadija, Khadijah, Khadeeja, Khatija, or Khatijah is a feminine given name of Arabic origin. It is the name of Khadija bint Khuwaylid, the first wife of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

khalid.a: Khalid or Xalîd is a masculine given name and surname of Arabic origin meaning "eternal, everlasting, immortal." Notable people with the name include:

khalil.a: Khalil or Khaleel means friend and is a common male first name in the Middle East, the Caucasus, the Balkans, North Africa, West Africa, East Africa, Central Asia and among Muslims in South Asia and as such is also a common surname.

kian.a: Kian is the English variant of the Gaelic Irish given name Cian, meaning 'ancient'. A variant spelling is Kyan. Kian is also a common Persian given name meaning 'king' or 'realm'.

kiana.e: Borrowed from Kiana, itself from English Diana. Also used as a modern feminine form of Kian.
kiana.a: Kiana or Kianna is a feminine given name with origins in multiple languages and cultures. It is sometimes regarded as a modern English name formed from the elements ki and ana or anna.

kiara.a: Kiara is a given name with various origins. It may be a variant of the Italian name Chiara, meaning bright, or the Irish name Ciara, meaning dark-haired. In Japan, Kiara is an uncommon name typically given to males; its meaning is dependent upon the characters used to spell the name.

kiera.a: Kiera is a female given name. It is an Anglicized version of Ciara, the name of a 7th-century saint, and means 'dark' or 'dark haired' in Irish.

kieran.a: Ciarán or Ciaran (Scottish Gaelic spelling) is a traditionally male given name of Irish and Scottish origin. It means "little dark one" or "little dark-haired one", produced by appending a diminutive suffix to ciar ("black", "dark"). It is the masculine version of the name Ciara.

kierra.a: Kierra (kee-er-rah) is a female given name. The name may be a variant of the Irish name Kiara meaning "dark" or a variant of the Greek name Kira meaning "lord". US usage of the name reached a peak in 1995.

kilian.a: Killian or Kilian, as a given name, is an Anglicized version of the Irish name Cillian. The name Cillian was borne by several early Irish saints including missionaries to Artois (France) and Franconia (Germany) and the author of the life of St Brigid.

killian.e: An anglicized spelling of Irish Cillian.
killian.a: Killian or Kilian, as a given name, is an Anglicized version of the Irish name Cillian. The name Cillian was borne by several early Irish saints including missionaries to Artois (France) and Franconia (Germany) and the author of the life of St Brigid.

king.a: King is the given name or nickname of:

kingsley.a: Kingsley is an English given name. Written in Old English as Cyningesleah, this locational name roughly means "from the king's wood, glade or meadow," and derives from the Old English words Cyning (King) and leah (woodland clearing).

kira.e: Variant of Kyra or Russian Ки́ра, ultimately from Persian کوروش. Also used as a respelling of Ciara.
kira.a: Kira is a mostly feminine name of multiple origins and meanings; in Japan, Kira is a unisex given name.

kit.a: Kit is a given name. It can be short for Christopher, Katherine, Kathleen, Kitty, among others.

kitty.a: Kitty or Kittie is a feminine given name, an English diminutive of Katherine or Irish diminutive of Caitlin and an extension of Kit.

knox.a: Knox is a primarily masculine given name, a transferred use of a Scottish surname and place name from the Scots Gaelic "cnoc" or Old English cnocc, referring to a small hill with a round top.

kobe.a: Kobe is a unisex given name that has multiple origins and meanings. Origins include Hebrew, Dutch, Swahili, Japanese, Akan and Greek origins. Alternate spellings of this name are Cobe, Cobie, Coby, Colbie, Colby, Koby, Kobbi and Kobi.

kobi.a: Kobi is a given name. It is an alternative spelling of Coby, which itself is a nickname for Jacob. Notable people with the name include:

koby.a: Coby or Koby is a male and female name, a surname, or a nickname originating from the name "Jacob" or "Jakob".

kristian.a: Kristian is a given name in several languages, and is a variant spelling of Christian.

kyla.e: Modern invention that can be explained as a feminine form of Kyle with -a.
kyla.a: Kyla is a female given name. It is a derivative of the originally Irish and Scottish Gaelic Kyle. Kyla may refer to:

kylan.e: Modern coinage; compare Kyle. Variant: Kylen.
kylan.a: Kylan is a unisex given name. Notable people with the given name include: Kylan Boswell (born 2005), American basketball player Kylan Darnell, American internet personality and Miss Ohio Teen USA 2022 Kylan Hamdaoui (born 1994), French rugby union player

kyle.e: From several places in Scotland and Northern Ireland, derived from Gaelic caol (“narrows”).
kyle.a: Kyle is a unisex English-language given name. It is a transferred use of the Scottish surname Kyle or of place names such as Kyle, Ayrshire on the southwest coast of Scotland. Kyle is also a Scots word for a strait, derived from the Gaelic caol ("narrow").

kylian.a: Killian or Kilian, as a given name, is an Anglicized version of the Irish name Cillian. The name Cillian was borne by several early Irish saints including missionaries to Artois (France) and Franconia (Germany) and the author of the life of St Brigid.

kylie.a: Kylie is an English feminine given name with multiple origins. It might be a variant of the name Kyle. It might be derived from the Aboriginal Australian Noongar word kiley, meaning 'curved, returning stick, boomerang'.

kylo.a: Kylo is a primarily masculine name usually given in reference to the Star Wars character Kylo Ren. Usage of the name has increased in the United States and United Kingdom and elsewhere.

kyra.e: Name of a Greek Orthodox saint, from κυρά (“lady”), or from Cyra, feminine form of Cyrus. The English name may also be a variant of Keira.
kyra.a: Kyra is a feminine given name that may derive from the Greek word kurá (meaning lady) or from Cyra, the feminine form of Cyrus.

kyran.a: Ciarán or Ciaran (Scottish Gaelic spelling) is a traditionally male given name of Irish and Scottish origin. It means "little dark one" or "little dark-haired one", produced by appending a diminutive suffix to ciar ("black", "dark"). It is the masculine version of the name Ciara.

kyrie.a: Kyrie is a unisex given name.

kyron.a: Kyron is a masculine given name.

lachlan.e: From Scottish Gaelic Lachlann, Lochlann (“land of the lochs, loch or fjord land, i.e. Scandinavia”), said to refer to an immigrant from Norway, a Norseman.
lachlan.a: Lachlan () is a masculine given name of Scottish Gaelic origin.

laiba.a: Laiba is a given name and surname. Notable people with the name include: Laiba Khan (born 1997), Pakistani actress Laiba Ahmed Mahloof (born 2013), Maldivian badminton player Haotak Laiba, legendary Indian king

laila.e: Variant of Leila and Layla, from Arabic لَيْلَى, related to لَيْلَة (“night”).
laila.a: Leila , also spelt Layla, is a feminine given name of Arabic origin. It is popular in the Middle East, including Arabic-speaking countries, Iran, Turkey, and Palestine, as well as the Nordic countries, India and the Anglosphere.

lainey.a: Lainey is a usually feminine given name or nickname with multiple origins and multiple spelling variants.

lana.e: Short form of Alana, or from Russian Ла́на, diminutive of several names including Светла́на.
lana.a: Lana is a female given name and short name of multiple origins.

lando.e: Two main origins: * Borrowed from Italian Lando, a patronymic surname from a personal name of origin. * Borrowed from Landó, a pet form of the personal name Lándor.
lando.a: Lando is both a masculine Italian given name, a nickname and a surname. Lando or Landó may refer to:

lara.e: Anglicized from Russian Ла́ра, a pet form of Larissa, known from the novel (1957) and film (1965) Dr Zhivago.
lara.a: Lara is a feminine given name or a surname in several languages. It can be used as a short form of the name Larissa. It was popularized in the Anglosphere by a character in the 1965 film Dr Zhivago.

laura.e: From Late saint's name Laura, from the feminine form of laurus (“laurel tree”). A post-classical name made famous by Petrarch's sonnets to Laura in the fourteenth century.
laura.a: Laura is a traditionally feminine given name in Europe and the Americas, of Latin origin, whose meaning ("bay laurel") is a metonym for a victor, and an early hypocorism from Laurel and Lauren.

lauren.a: Lauren is mostly a feminine given name. The name's meaning may be "laurel tree", "sweet of honor", or "wisdom". It is derived from the French name Laurence, a feminine version of Laurent, which is in turn derived from the Roman surname Laurentius.

laurence.e: From the name of a third century Roman martyr, Latin Laurentius, "a person from Laurentum", the place name possibly derived from laurus (“laurel”).
laurence.a: Laurence is in modern use as an English masculine and a French feminine given name. The modern English masculine name is a variant of Lawrence and originates from a French form of the Latin Laurentius, a name meaning "man from Laurentum".

laurie.e: The given names are s of ie, all ultimately from Latin laurus (“laurel”).
laurie.a: Laurie is a unisex given name. Among males, it can be a short form (hypocorism) of Lawrence, Laurence or Laurens. For females, it can be a short form of Lauren or Laura.

lavinia.e: Latin Lavinia, of obscure meaning. Lavinium was a town in ancient Latium.
lavinia.a: Lavinia is a feminine given name which may refer to: Lavinia Blackwall, member of the Scottish folk rock group Trembling Bells (formed 2008) Lavinia Burnett , first woman to be executed in the state of Arkansas Lavinia Byrne (born 1948), Roman Catholic former nun Lavinia Crosse , English founder of…

lawrence.a: Lawrence is a masculine given name. It is an Anglicisation of the French Laurent, which is in turn derived from the Latin Laurentius or Old Greek Lavrenti . Pet forms of Lawrence include Larry, Lawrie and, less commonly, Law.

lawson.a: Lawson is a masculine given name borne by: Lawson Aschenbach (born 1983), American racing driver Lawson Butt , British actor and director of the silent era Lawson Craddock (born 1992), American former road and track racing cyclist Lawson Crouse (born 1997), Canadian ice hockey player in the…

layan.a: Layan is a feminine Arabic given name meaning "prosperity life", "soft, gentle." Leen is a related name. Both are among the most popular names given to newborn girls in the Arab world in the past decade.

layla.e: One of many of a name transliterated from Arabic; see Leila for more information. Since the late 20th century, in English, this given name in this spelling is sometimes bestowed solely because it is considered euphonious, a theme true of…
layla.a: Leila , also spelt Layla, is a feminine given name of Arabic origin. It is popular in the Middle East, including Arabic-speaking countries, Iran, Turkey, and Palestine, as well as the Nordic countries, India and the Anglosphere.

layton.a: Layton is a masculine given name which may refer to: Layton Freborg (born 1933), American politician Layton Kor , American rock climber Layton Maxwell (born 1979), Welsh footballer Layton Williams (born 1994), English actor Layton Ratings (born 2009 or whatever) English Clown

lea.a: Lea is a feminine given name. In French, the name Léa is from the biblical name Leah. In Spanish, the same name is Lía, and in Italian, Lia.

leah.a: Leah is a feminine given name of Hebrew origin. Its meaning is often deciphered as "delicate" or "weary". The name can be traced back to the Biblical matriarch Leah, one of the two wives of Jacob.

lee.e: From Old English lēa, the dative case of lēah (“meadow”), originally to denote someone who lived near a meadow.
lee.a: Lee is a unisex given name from the English word 'lee'. It is also used as a surname, often confused with the Old English surname and given name leah ("clearing; meadow"), which evolved to 'leigh' in Middle English, and present-day 'lea' with the same meaning.

leen.a: Leen is a name of multiple origins. It is a popular Arabic name for girls meaning “tender” and “delicate”. It is spelled لِينٌ in Arabic and has been translated into English in multiple spellings.

leena.a: Leena is a feminine given name. It is a variant spelling of Lina and Lena. It is a direct Quranic Arabic name, meaning "young palm tree", or figuratively "tender, young, delicate".

leia.e: From the name of a princess in the American fantasy film Star Wars (1977).

leighton.e: Various place names in England, Old English leac (“leek”) + tun (“settlement”), also in the sense of a herb garden.

leila.e: From Arabic لَيْلَى. Taken into English usage through nineteenth-century literature.
leila.a: Leila , also spelt Layla, is a feminine given name of Arabic origin. It is popular in the Middle East, including Arabic-speaking countries, Iran, Turkey, and Palestine, as well as the Nordic countries, India and the Anglosphere.

leilani.a: Leilani is a Hawaiian given name meaning "heavenly garland of flowers" or "royal child". The Hawaiian word lei refers to flowers and lani to the sky or heavens, with an association to royalty.

lena.e: The female name is from the Scandinavian, German and Russian pet form of Helena, Magdalena and Yelena (also spelled Elena).
lena.a: Lena is a feminine given name, a short form of Helena , meaning 'torch' or 'shining light'. It may be a given name by itself or a diminutive of Helena and variants, such as Elena.

leni.a: Leni is both a given name and a surname. Notable people with the name include:

lennie.a: Lenny or Lennie is a given name. Notable people with the name include:

lennon.e: From Irish Ó Leannáin (“descendant of Lover (Leannán)”) and from Ó Lonáin (“descendant of Blackbird (Lonán)”).
lennon.a: The name Lennon or Lennan is both a surname and a given name that has grown in popularity in English-speaking countries in recent years for both boys and girls. Origins include Irish Ó Leannáin ("descendant of Lover (leannán)") and from Ó Lionáin ("descendant of Blackbird (Lonán)").

lennox.a: Lennox or Lenox is the given name of:

lenny.a: Lenny or Lennie is a given name. Notable people with the name include:

leo.e: From Latin leō (“lion”), Ancient Greek λέων, /.
leo.a: Leo is a given name in several languages. In European languages, it is usually a masculine given name and it comes from the Latin word leo, which in turn comes from the Greek word λέων meaning "lion".

leon.e: Ultimately from Latin Leo and leo (“lion”), from Ancient Greek Λέων and λέων (“lion”), likely ultimately from a non-Indo-European language.
leon.a: Leon is a first name of Greek origin, meaning "lion". It gave rise to similar names in other languages, including the Latin Leo, French Lyon or Léon, Irish Leon, Spanish León, Armenian Levon / Լևոն or Georgian Levan / ლევან. In Greek mythology, Leon was a giant killed by Heracles.

leona.a: Leona is a female given name derived from the Latin word leo for "lion". People and fictional characters named Leona include:

leonard.e: From Old French Leonard, name of a 6th century Frankish saint, from Old High German leo (“lion”) or Old High German liut (“person”) and hart (“hard”). As a surname, also used as an anglicisation of Irish Ó Leannáin (Lennon).
leonard.a: Leonard is a common English surname and a masculine given name. The given name and surname originate from the Old High German Leonhard containing the prefix levon ("lion") from the Greek Λέων ("lion") through the Latin Leo, and the suffix hardu ("brave" or "hardy").

leonardo.a: Leonardo is a masculine given name, the Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese equivalent of the English, German, and Dutch name, Leonard. Notable people with the name include:

leonidas.e: From Ancient Greek Λεωνίδᾱς (“son of Leon / lion”).
leonidas.a: Leonidas is a masculine given name mainly in Greece. People with the name include:

leonie.e: From French Léonie, from Latin Leonia, feminine of Leonius, derived from leo (“lion”).
leonie.a: Leonie or (in French) Léonie or (in German) Leonie or in Arabic liuni is a Latin-origin feminine given name meaning "lioness", from the masculine personal name Leon (meaning "lion"). It is rare as a surname.

leonora.e: From the short form of Eleonora, cognate to Eleanor.
leonora.a: Leonora is a feminine given name which is a variation of Eleanor. It was relatively common in the 19th century in Western countries, ranking as the 314th most popular female given name in the United States in 1880. The name has declined in popularity but remains in use.

levi.e: Ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי, of uncertain origin.
levi.a: Levi is a masculine given name of Hebrew origin. It is the name of the biblical figure Levi , son of Jacob and founder of the Israelite tribe of Levi. The name is derived from the Hebrew verb לוה ("Lava"), meaning "to join" or "connect".

lewis.e: From Middle English Lewis, Lowis, from Old French Louis, from *Hlūdawīg.
lewis.a: Lewis () is a masculine English-language given name.

leyla.a: Leila , also spelt Layla, is a feminine given name of Arabic origin. It is popular in the Middle East, including Arabic-speaking countries, Iran, Turkey, and Palestine, as well as the Nordic countries, India and the Anglosphere.

lia.a: Lia is a feminine given name. In the Spanish-speaking world, it is accented Lía. In English-speaking countries, the name may be a variant of Leah or Lea.

liadan.a: Líadan is a feminine given name in the Irish language. One possible meaning is gray. Líadan or Liadan may refer to:

liana.a: Liana is a female given name. It is a short form of Eliana, Juliana, Liliana, Liyana and other names that end in -liana. It can also be a botanical name derived from Liana.

libby.a: Libby as a feminine given name is typically a diminutive form of Elizabeth, which is less commonly spelled 'Libbie' or 'Libi'. In recent years, it has been used as a shortened version of the name Liberty.

lila.e: Variant of Leila or Lilah, depending on pronunciation; also associated with Spanish lila (“lilac”).
lila.a: Lila is a feminine given name.

lilah.e: Short form of Delilah; also a variant of Leila.

lili.a: Lili is a feminine given name.

lilia.e: Borrowed from Latin lilia, plural of lilium (“lily”), or a Latinization of the English Lily.
lilia.a: Lilia is a feminine given name.

lilian.e: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of Elizabeth, but generally accepted as a variant of lilium (“lily”).
lilian.a: Lillian, also spelled Lilian, Lilliann, or Lilliane, is a female given name. Its origin is the Latin word Lilium (lily). In French, Lilian is the male form of the name, while Liliane is the female form.

lilith.a: Lilith is a feminine given name sometimes given in reference to Lilith, a character in Jewish folklore who was said to be the first wife of the first man Adam who disobeyed him, was banished from the Garden of Eden, and who became a mythical she-demon.

lillian.e: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of Elizabeth, but generally accepted as a variant of Late Latin lilium (“lily”).
lillian.a: Lillian, also spelled Lilian, Lilliann, or Lilliane, is a female given name. Its origin is the Latin word Lilium (lily). In French, Lilian is the male form of the name, while Liliane is the female form.

lillie.a: Lillie is both a surname and a given name. Notable people with the name include:

lilly.a: Lilly is a feminine given name which is borne by:

lily.e: A 19th-century flower name, from lily. Also a diminutive of Lilian and sometimes Elizabeth.
lily.a: Lily is a feminine given name usually derived from lily, the flower. The name became particularly popular along with other flower names for girls during the 1800s and early 1900s. The lily also has associations with and has been symbolic of innocence and purity in Christian art.

lina.e: Short form of any female name ending in -lina, such as Angelina, Carolina, Evelina. It can also be construed as a rare feminine form of Linus.
lina.a: Lina is a feminine given name with many origins in different nations.

lincoln.e: Middle English Lincolne, from Old English Lincolle, Lindcolen, Lindcylene, from Latin Lindum Colōnia (“the Roman settlement Lindum Colonia”), from *llɨnn (“pool”), from Proto-Celtic *lindos (“lake, liquid”), in reference to the Brayford.
lincoln.a: Lincoln is a male given name, and according to US data based on 2024 births, about 1 in 376 people are given the name. Lincoln is also a surname and sometimes masculine given name of Old English origin.

lisa.e: Diminutive of Elisabeth in several European languages. The computer is named after Lisa Brennan-Jobs, officially explained as an acronym for “Locally Integrated Software Architecture”.
lisa.a: Lisa is a feminine given name. In the United Kingdom, the name Lisa began to gain popularity during the 1960s, by 1974 it was the fifth most popular female name there, and a decade later it was the 14th most popular female name there. However, by 1996 it had fallen out of the top 100.

livia.e: From Latin Līvia, feminine form of Līvius, name of a plebeian Roman gens.
livia.a: Livia was the wife of Augustus and the most powerful woman in the early Roman Empire. Livia is a female name of Latin origin, meaning "blue," or of Hebrew origin meaning "garland." From Roman times, this was the female derivative of the family name Livius.

lochlainn.a: Lachlan () is a masculine given name of Scottish Gaelic origin.

lochlann.a: Lachlan () is a masculine given name of Scottish Gaelic origin.

lockie.a: Lockie is a surname and a given name. The surname is a variant of the surname Lucas. The given name is a nickname of the given name Lachlan.

logan.a: The given name Logan is derived from the Scottish surname Logan, which is in turn derived from a place-name. The likely origin of this surname is a place located near Auchinleck, in Ayrshire.

lois.e: From Ancient Greek Λωΐς, of obscure meaning. Unrelated to Louise or Louisa.

loki.e: Old Norse Loki, where further etymology is shown.

lola.a: Lola is a feminine given name and nickname in the Romance languages, and other language groups. It is a hypocoristic form of the Spanish name Dolores, meaning "sorrows", taken from one of the titles of the Virgin Mary: Nuestra Señora de los Dolores, or Our Lady of Sorrows.

lorcan.a: Lorcan is a male given name, meaning 'little fierce one', and may refer to: Lorcan Allen (born 1940), Irish farmer and former Fianna Fáil Teachta Dála TD Lorcan Cranitch (born 1959), Irish actor Lorcan Dempsey (born 1958), the Vice President and Chief Strategist of the Online Computer Library…

lorena.e: From, by folk etymology associated with Laura. Henry Webster's title for his song was inspired by Edgar Allan Poe's Lenore.
lorena.a: Lorena is a German, English, Croatian, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish feminine given name with different origins. It can be used as a version of Lorraine or, alternately, as a Latin version of Lauren. As a Croatian, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish name, it is derived from the Latin Laurentius.

lorenzo.a: Lorenzo is an Italian and Spanish masculine given name of Latin origin. It is used in Italy, Spain, and other Spanish-speaking countries. The name was derived from the Roman surname Laurentius.

lottie.a: Lottie is an English feminine given name that is a diminutive form of Charlotte, Lieselotte, or Ottilie. It is an alternate form of Lotte, and that is also related to Lisa, Elisa and Elisabeth. Notable people with the name include the following:

louie.a: Louie has historically been regarded as a less common variant of the given name Louis. It originated in the United Kingdom as a more regularly-spelled version without a silent ⟨s⟩. In 2011, it was the 74th most common forename for births in England and Wales, with Louis slightly more common at 68th.

louis.e: From French Louis, from Middle French Loïs, Loïc, &c., from Old French Looïs, Luis, Lodhuvigs, Lodevis, Lodhwig, &c., from Latin Ludovicus, from Clodovicus, from *Hlūdawīg, from Proto-Germanic *hlūdaz (“loud; famous”) + *wīgą (“battle”).
louis.a: Louis is the French form of the Old Frankish given name Chlodwig and one of two English forms, the other being Lewis ().

louise.e: From French Louise, the feminine form of Louis.
louise.a: Louise and Luise are, respectively, French and German feminine forms of the given name Louis. Louise has been regularly used as a female name in English-speaking countries since the middle of the 19th century.

luca.e: Borrowed from Italian Luca, from Latin Lūcās, from Ancient Greek Λουκᾶς, hypocoristic of Λούκιος (from Latin Lūcius) or Λουκανός or both with -ᾶς.

lucas.e: From Latin Lucas, from Ancient Greek Λουκᾶς. See the Greek entry for more.
lucas.a: Lucas is a multilingual masculine given name of Latin origin. It is derived from the Latin verb "lucere", meaning "to shine". Lucas is used as a given name in Greek, English, Spanish, French, Dutch, and Portuguese.

lucia.e: Latinate variant of Lucy, or today borrowed from modern Italian. Name of a Sicilian martyr, Latin Lūcia, feminine form of the Roman praenomen Lūcius.
lucia.a: Lucia is both a feminine given name and a surname. It comes from the Latin word Lux meaning 'light'. It is the feminine form of the Roman praenomen Lucius and can be alternatively spelled as Lucy.

lucian.e: From Latin Lūcianus, either a derivative of the Roman praenomen Lūcius, from lūx (“light”); or from Ancient Greek Λουκιανός, of obscure meaning.

luciano.a: Luciano is an Italian, Spanish and Portuguese given name and surname. It is derived from Latin Lucianus, patronymic of Lucius ("Light"). The French form is Lucien, the Catalan version is Llucià while the Basque form is Luken.

lucie.a: Lucie is the French and Czech form of the female name Lucia. It is also a nickname or hypocorism. It may refer to:

lucy.e: From Middle English Lucy, from Old French Lucie (notably after the Christian martyr Lucia of Syracuse), from Latin Lucia (feminine of Lucius, a Roman praenomen), from lux (“light”).
lucy.a: Lucy is an English feminine given name derived from the Latin masculine given name Lucius with the meaning as of light (born at dawn or daylight, maybe also shiny, or of light complexion). Alternative spellings are Luci and Lucie.

lughaidh.e: From Old Irish Lugaid, from Proto-Celtic *Lugudeks (“one who serves the god Lugus”) from *Lugus + *dekos, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱos (“that which is proper”). Compare Lucudeca.

luis.a: Luis is a given name. It is the Spanish form of the originally Germanic name Hludowig or Chlodovech, which were introduced to the Iberian Peninsula during its occupation by the Visigoths.

luisa.e: From Old French Louise, feminine of Louis, further traced to Latin Ludovicus. Cognate with Spanish Luisa and French Louisa.
luisa.a: Luisa (Italian and Spanish) or Luísa (Portuguese) is a feminine given name; it is the feminine form of the given name Louis (Luis), the French form of the Frankish Chlodowig (German Ludwig), from the Germanic elements hlod "fame" and wig "combat".

luka.e: From the common Slavic (, etc) male given name Luka and from Лука́, all cognates of English Luke and Lucas.
luka.a: Luka is a Slavic masculine given name. In Japanese: ルカ, るか is transliterated Luka or Ruka, and can be masculine or feminine (possibly related to Haruka). The male name Luka comes from the Latin word "Lucanus" which means a man from Lucania.

luke.e: From Latin Lūcās, from Λουκᾶς. See the Greek entry for more.
luke.a: Luke () is a masculine given name and, less commonly, a surname. The name Luke is the English form and the diminutive of the Latin name Lucas. The exact etymology of the name is contested.

luna.e: From Middle English lune, luna (“the moon”), from Latin lūna/Lūna, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂.
luna.a: Luna is a feminine given name of Latin origin, meaning moon. In Roman mythology, Luna was the divine personification of the Moon.

lydia.e: Ancient Greek Λυδία (“the region of Lydia”), from λυδία (“beautiful one, noble one”), a feminine form of Λυδός (Lydus, from λυδός (lydus)). The region of Lydia is said to be named for a king Λυδός (Lydus, from λυδός (lydus))
lydia.a: Lydia is a feminine first name. It derives from the Greek Λυδία, Ludía, from λυδία (ludía; "beautiful one", "noble one", "from Lydia"), a feminine form of the ancient given name Λυδός (Lydus).

lyra.e: Borrowed from Latin Lyra/lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρα (“a lyre; the constellation Lyra”).
